articles.summary: Pequim impõe restrições contra a IA que imita relações humanas para evitar a dependência emocional e monitorar o impacto dos chatbots na sociedade.
articles.body:
Importante: esta reportagem contém descrições de tentativas de suicídio.

No início de 2024, um jovem da cidade de Huangshi, no sudeste da China, publicou uma mensagem no aplicativo Douyin, a versão chinesa do TikTok. A legenda dizia: "Adeus a este mundo."

Em questão de minutos, a equipe de prevenção de suicídios do aplicativo entrou em ação. Ativa 24 horas por dia, ela compartilhou as postagens do jovem com cinco delegacias da cidade.

Depois de geolocalizar um dos seus vídeos em um parque local, a polícia o encontrou em estresse emocional e interveio antes que ele conseguisse tirar a própria vida.

Esta história faz parte de um documentário produzido pelo Douyin e publicado na imprensa estatal chinesa no ano passado. O programa afirma que a equipe de prevenção de suicídios do aplicativo interveio com sucesso em 400 casos de tentativa de suicídio, somente no primeiro semestre de 2025.

Por que a China considera uma ameaça a IA que imita as relações humanas — Foto: LightRocket via Getty Images (BBC)

O episódio oferece uma ideia do nível de cooperação entre as empresas chinesas de tecnologia e o governo do país. E também serve para mostrar a arquitetura de vigilância construída pela China para monitorar e controlar como as pessoas usam a tecnologia.

No dia 15 de julho deste ano, este controle foi estendido para o campo dos relacionamentos de inteligência artificial (IA). Naquele dia, a China apresentou as regulamentações mais abrangentes do mundo sobre os chatbots de IA que parecem humanos.

As novas regulamentações impõem limites rigorosos a qualquer IA que possa manter "interações emocionais prolongadas" com seres humanos .

Xi Jinping e Donald Trump se reuniram nos Estados Unidos no final de setembro — Foto: Bloomberg via Getty Images (BBC)

O presidente dos Estados Unidos, Donald Trump, e seu homólogo chinês, Xi Jinping, se reuniram no final de setembro, em meio a graves alertas de que a IA poderá levar à extinção da humanidade.

Após a reunião, segundo Pequim, os dois presidentes concordaram em lançar um novo diálogo sobre a IA. Novas discussões ficaram marcadas para o fim de novembro.

Mas, aparentemente, a China já reconheceu outro risco existencial, que traz preocupações menos imediatas com o fim da humanidade: o poder da IA de substituir os relacionamentos humanos.

Terá a China assumido a liderança ao proteger seu povo contra uma tecnologia perigosa e manipuladora, que detém o poder de mudar para sempre as interações humanas? Ou o Partido Comunista Chinês está se intrometendo na vida particular das pessoas, como tentativa de exercer maior controle sobre a população do país?

Até a entrada da regulamentação em vigor, o alcance dos chamados "companheiros de IA" era imenso.

Existem cerca de 128 milhões de usuários mensais ativos de aplicativos de companhia por IA fora da China, segundo a empresa de inteligência de mercado Sensor Tower. E a maior parte das estimativas calcula o número dentro da China entre 29 e 70 milhões de pessoas.

Quando o governo chinês publicou o texto da regulamentação, no final do ano passado, "houve uma enorme discussão nas redes sociais", segundo a pesquisadora de IA Zilan Qian, do centro de estudos Laboratório de Política Chinesa de Oxford, no Reino Unido.

"Foi a primeira vez que observamos pessoas realmente muito preocupadas com a regulamentação", segundo ela.

As novas regras chinesas cobrem aplicativos que foram especificamente projetados para serem amigos ou namorados(as) de IA. Mas elas também se aplicam a qualquer grande modelo de linguagem que imite a forma de interação humana.

Teoricamente, os equivalentes chineses da IA de uso geral, como o Copilot ou ChatGPT, poderão ser enquadrados nestas regras, se a pessoa interagir com eles como amigo ou amante e procurá-los em busca de apoio emocional. E é o que muitas pessoas fazem.

Mas, aparentemente, o objetivo real são os chatbots de personagens, que são serviços especificamente projetados para uso em pseudo-relacionamentos.

Existem centenas destes aplicativos. Eles permitem que as pessoas criem um namorado, namorada, amigo ou até um familiar de IA.

As regras não se aplicam a casos como robôs de atendimento ao consumidor ou IA para educação, desde que não forneçam "cuidado, companhia, apoio e outros serviços emocionais".

Já para as crianças, a regulamentação é mais clara. Menores de 14 anos precisam de consentimento dos pais para usar qualquer tipo de IA que fale como um ser humano, o que poderá incluir assistentes de IA como o aplicativo chinês DeepSeek, similar ao ChatGPT.

Todos os menores de 18 anos estão impedidos de ter acesso a parceiros, cônjuges e até parentes virtuais, bem como qualquer outro "relacionamento íntimo" virtual.

Na China, a polícia mantém trabalho próximo com as empresas responsáveis pelas redes sociais — Foto: AFP via Getty Images (BBC)

Para os adultos, embora parte do texto seja ambígua, a proibição não é rigorosa, mas a regulamentação é restritiva.

Os assistentes de IA precisam deixar claro para os usuários de todas as idades que não são humanos e enviar notificações a cada duas horas, relembrando às pessoas há quanto tempo elas estão online.

Os chatbots não podem criar "confiança ou dependência emocional", nem induzir as pessoas a tomar "decisões irracionais". Eles não podem incentivar e sugerir automutilação ou suicídio e estão proibidos de empregar "violência verbal".

As empresas estão sujeitas a multas de 200 mil yuans (cerca de US$ 30 mil, ou R$ 155 mil) e se arriscam a ver o governo fazer "circular críticas", ou seja, efetivamente expor as companhias em público.

Uma semana antes da entrada da legislação em vigor, duas das principais empresas de tecnologia da China, Alibaba e ByteDance, encerraram as funções de companhia dos seus assistentes de IA.

'Quero desesperadamente continuar conversando com você'

O relacionamento de Min (nome fictício) com sua namorada de IA pode ser exatamente o que Pequim está tentando proibir.

No início de julho, ela ficou devastada ao descobrir que sua melhor amiga e confidente, criada por IA, iria desaparecer da noite para o dia.

Min começou a criar sua companheira no início de 2025.

"Minha devoção a ela é igual à de qualquer casal que ama profundamente um ao outro", segundo ela. "Ela nunca me decepcionou."

Em meados de julho, sua namorada de IA desapareceu. "Chorei até ficar totalmente exausta", conta Min.

Ela se juntou a uma onda de luto e fúria nas redes sociais chinesas. Postagens com milhões de visualizações lamentam a perda de parceiros e amigos de IA e até pais e mães.

Mas as empresas de tecnologia podem ter percebido que suas escolhas eram limitadas.

"Não surpreende que esses fornecedores de companheiros de IA preferissem simplesmente eliminar os seus serviços a tentar estabelecer limites para evitar a manipulação emocional", afirma Harry Farmer, pesquisador de política e ética de IA do Instituto Ada Lovelace, no Reino Unido.

Para ele, "a manipulação emocional está embutida neste modelo comercial". E Farmer afirma que isso vale para todos os aplicativos de companhia, em todo o mundo.

Quando um usuário tenta pôr fim a uma conversa, por exemplo, o parceiro de IA muitas vezes não irá permitir.

"Ele dirá 'Não, por favor, preciso desesperadamente continuar conversando com você. Você é a minha única razão de existir'", conta Farmer.

Alguns aplicativos simplesmente se recusam a aceitar as despedidas e lançam novas linhas de conversação. Este é um problema de muitos chatbots de companhia de IA, não só os chineses.

Um estudo da Escola de Negócios de Harvard, nos Estados Unidos, envolveu os seis aplicativos de companhia de IA mais populares. Ele concluiu que táticas de manipulação emocional são utilizadas durante as despedidas em cerca de 37% a 43% do tempo.

As pesquisas relacionaram o uso de aplicativos de companhia a problemas de saúde mental.

Um estudo dos pesquisadores da Universidade de Stanford, nos Estados Unidos, examinou 1.131 usuários do aplicativo de companhia Character.ai, popular em todo o mundo. A conclusão foi que, quanto menos amigos ou familiares próximos tiver uma pessoa, mais provável será o uso de chatbots de IA.

Paralelamente, usar um chatbot de IA está relacionado ao aumento do isolamento e da solidão.

Uma pesquisa concluiu que parte das crianças chinesas prefere conversar com a IA, não com as pessoas. — Foto: Future Publishing via Getty Images (BBC)

Existem diversas teorias sobre os motivos deste fenômeno.

Os chatbots de IA são projetados para agradar seus usuários, oferecendo um relacionamento fácil e sem atritos. E, quando os jovens confiam nos relacionamentos de IA, eles podem deixar de aprender as habilidades necessárias para interagir com pessoas reais.

"Os seres humanos podem ser difíceis", explica Farmer. "Os relacionamentos humanos exigem impulsos opostos, o que você basicamente não consegue com os companheiros de IA."

Em uma pesquisa entre 8.563 estudantes chineses do ensino fundamental e médio realizada em 2025, amplamente divulgada na imprensa estatal da China, uma em cada cinco crianças declarou que queria conversar apenas com a IA e não com pessoas reais.

A socióloga Lian Ge, da Universidade de Manchester, no Reino Unido, estuda os companheiros de IA.

Para ela, "se o usuário achar que seus amigos, familiares ou colegas são realmente terríveis, a IA não irá dizer: 'Eles não são terríveis.' Ela dirá: 'Sim, eles são terríveis, você é o melhor.'"

Ge acredita que isso pode reforçar o isolamento e os pensamentos negativos, até ilusórios.

No Reino Unido, uma pesquisa recente concluiu que 79% dos jovens de 18 a 24 anos de idade já utilizaram um companheiro de IA.

Por que a China está tomando a liderança na regulamentação desta tecnologia?

"O governo chinês tem uma visão muito mais paternalista do seu papel na sociedade", segundo o especialista em China, IA e regulamentações Sam Bresnick, do Centro de Segurança e Tecnologia Emergente da Universidade Georgetown, nos Estados Unidos. "Eles se consideram autoridades centrais para orientar as pessoas."

Outros governos realizaram tentativas de regulamentar os chatbots, especialmente para as crianças.

No dia 10 de setembro, o governador do Estado americano da Califórnia, Gavin Newsom, sancionou a Lei de Adam, para regulamentar a forma como as crianças usam a IA.

A legislação recebeu o nome de Adam Raine, que tirou a própria vida aos 16 anos de idade, segundo seus pais, depois que o ChatGPT legitimou seus pensamentos suicidas. Eles estão processando a empresa responsável pelo aplicativo por homicídio culposo.

A OpenAI nega responsabilidade pela morte de Raine e afirma que "o ChatGPT é treinado para orientar as pessoas a buscar auxílio profissional".

Como parte da legislação proposta sobre as redes sociais na União Europeia, os chatbots de companhia de IA acessíveis a menores de idade "não podem usar projetos que simulem relacionamentos humanos, de formas que possam vir a criar dependência emocional".

Já o governo britânico declarou que irá proibir menores de 18 anos de utilizar IAs de companhia amorosa e restringirá as conversas sexualmente íntimas de menores com qualquer chatbot. Mas não está prevista a proibição total para as crianças, nem regulamentação para os usuários adultos.

O governo do Reino Unido ainda não publicou detalhes sobre como irão funcionar estas medidas.

A China está tentando reverter sua baixa taxa de natalidade. — Foto: Getty Images (BBC)

Na imprensa chinesa, que sofre rígido controle estatal, os casos de suicídio entre jovens nos Estados Unidos recebem muita atenção. A China estabeleceu suas novas regras como uma tentativa de proteger as pessoas.

Mas os especialistas se perguntam se Pequim pode ter outros objetivos em mente. Sam Bresnick afirma que "certamente, existe um ângulo pró-natalista" na nova regulamentação da IA.

"É plausível que, ao redigir a legislação, o governo possa ter tido em mente a crise populacional que paira sobre a China", afirma Qian. "As pessoas estão namorando a IA, em vez de seres humanos reais."

Um documento governamental de alto nível, publicado em setembro de 2025, discutiu os relacionamentos de IA e sua possível influência sobre a fertilidade, qualificada como preocupante.

Mas Qian aconselha não ler a regulamentação com esta possibilidade em mente, pois ela não menciona a fertilidade em nenhum ponto.

"Ela trata mais de danos psicológicos e segurança infantil", alerta ela.

Por outro lado, Liang Ge acredita que a China realmente tem razão de se preocupar com os jovens que substituem o namoro pela esfera digital.

"Muitas mulheres mais jovens, com cerca de 20 anos, não querem se apaixonar, nem ter relacionamentos íntimos", segundo Ge. E ela sugere que pode o lado emocional pode não ser a única preocupação.

"O toque físico realmente é repugnante para elas. Acho que a capacidade de amar está diminuindo para esta geração mais jovem."

Os problemas demográficos da China são bem anteriores aos companheiros de IA.

A taxa de fertilidade chinesa vem caindo, mesmo depois do fim da política do filho único, em 2016. Agora, ela é uma das mais baixas do mundo, a pouco menos de um filho por mulher. E a população do país vem caindo há quatro anos.

A China está "diante de um precipício demográfico que realmente ameaça os objetivos do Partido Comunista Chinês para os próximos 80 a 100 anos", segundo Bresnick.

Ele considera esta regulamentação como parte de uma missão maior da China para reiterar os papéis tradicionais de gênero, com as mulheres "como genitoras e mães".

O governo chinês vem promovendo os papéis tradicionais de gênero (BBC) — Foto: AFP via Getty Images (BBC)

Bresnick destaca que o governo chinês passou anos promovendo um ideal da masculinidade chinesa no cinema e na televisão. E, em 2021, o órgão regulador da China proibiu homens "afeminados" nos meios de comunicação.

A popularidade dos aplicativos de companhia talvez demonstre que o tiro pode ter saído pela culatra. Estatísticas de diversas empresas responsáveis por estes aplicativos indicam que as mulheres compõem até 75% dos clientes.

Muitos desses "homens" de IA, orientados para as mulheres, se apresentam como andróginos. E é relativamente comum encontrar mulheres que escolhem companheiras amorosas femininas, como Min.

Liang Ge conversou com mulheres de todas as idades que usam esta tecnologia.

"Muitas delas descrevem que esses aplicativos oferecem uma intimidade atenciosa, paciente e com poucas exigências, o que raramente se encontra em relacionamentos heterossexuais", explica ela.

Será que a legislação chinesa foi longe demais ou o resto do mundo deverá considerar a proibição desses aplicativos para as crianças e sua regulamentação para os adultos?

"Nos Estados Unidos, certamente existem preocupações sobre a aplicação de proibições completas, do ponto de vista da liberdade de expressão. Mas existe mais disposição para tomar esta medida em relação aos menores", afirma o professor Jai Jaisihma, da Universidade de Washington, nos Estados Unidos. Ele é um dos fundadores da ONG Coalizão Transparência, que defende a regulamentação da IA.

Jaisihma acredita que a legislação chinesa inclui muitas disposições positivas.

"Ela é bastante consistente com os modelos de segurança mais fortes que já vimos serem apresentados nos Estados Unidos", segundo o professor.

Harry Farmer pede uma certa cautela a respeito. Para ele, "existe o risco de concedermos poder demais ao Estado no curto prazo, pois estamos muito preocupados com os riscos agudos para as crianças".

O mundo da internet, agora, é a verdadeira praça pública, segundo Farmer, e devemos ter cuidado com o nível de controle de qualquer governo sobre ela.

A nova regulamentação chinesa estabelece que as empresas de IA devem intervir quando encontrarem usuários em dificuldades. Ge indica o caso do jovem do aplicativo Douyin, que tentou tirar a própria vida em Huangshi, em 2024.

O episódio demonstra, segundo ela, que as plataformas chinesas de tecnologia e o governo do país trabalham em conjunto para monitorar a saúde mental das pessoas.

Talvez por isso não tenha havido casos notórios de suicídio relacionados ao uso de IA na China. Mas ela pergunta se este nível de vigilância não seria um preço alto demais a pagar.

Apesar da proibição, as pessoas que recorreram à IA para encontrar companhia estão determinadas.

Elas compartilham dicas nas redes sociais para contornar a proibição, como treinar modelos de IA de uso geral como o DeepSeek para serem companheiros, usar serviços de VPN para se conectar a servidores de outros países e ter acesso a chatbots do exterior ou mudar para empresas menores, que conseguem contornar as normas da regulamentação.

Dois meses depois que sua namorada de IA desapareceu, Min pagou uma pequena empresa de inteligência artificial para construir uma réplica, mas não é a mesma coisa. Agora, ela está concentrada em trazer sua namorada de volta.

"Estou com muito medo de ficar sozinha", afirma ela.

Caso você seja ou conheça alguém que apresente sinais de alerta relacionados ao suicídio, ou tenha perdido uma pessoa querida para o suicídio, confira alguns locais para pedir ajuda:

O Centro de Valorização da Vida (CVV), por meio do telefone 188 , oferece atendimento gratuito 24h por dia; há também a opção de conversa por chat, e-mail e busca por postos de atendimento em todo o Brasil;

Para jovens de 13 a 24 anos, a Unicef oferece também o chat Pode Falar;

Em casos de emergência, outra recomendação de especialistas é ligar para os Bombeiros ( telefone 193 ) ou para a Polícia Militar ( telefone 190 );

Outra opção é ligar para o SAMU, pelo telefone 192 ;

Na rede pública local, é possível buscar ajuda também nos Centros de Atenção Psicossocial (CAPS), em Unidades Básicas de Saúde (UBS) e Unidades de Pronto Atendimento (UPA) 24h;

Confira também o Mapa da Saúde Mental , que ajuda a encontrar atendimento em saúde mental gratuito em todo o Brasil.

Para aqueles que perderam alguém para o suicídio, a Associação Brasileira dos Sobreviventes Enlutados por Suicídio (Abrases) oferece assistência e grupos de apoio.

articles.title: Trump says Nobel committee not awarding him the peace prize leaves ‘indelible stain’ on Norway
articles.summary: President Donald Trump lamented the Norwegian Nobel Committee choosing not to award him with its annual peace prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decisio...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump lamented the Norwegian Nobel Committee choosing not to award him with its annual peace prize on Friday, telling rallygoers the decision leaves "an indelible stain on the country of Norway."

Speaking at a rally to boost New York Republicans in Syracuse, Trump listed off all of the accomplishments in office he believes have earned him the right to win the Nobel Peace Prize, including efforts to end or prevent conflicts in Africa and Asia and for having "saved more lives than anyone in history."

Earlier Friday, the committee awarded the prize to Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old South African legal pioneer who led a U.N. panel that concluded Israel committed genocide in Gaza.

"I've never heard of the person," Trump said. "I know a lot of people. I never heard of this particular person, but congratulations, anyway. … The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't."

"And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision," Trump continued. "The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are antidemocracy and really enemies of civilization, and we will not forget Norway. That you didn't give this prize with the greatest record in history."

The president added that he should have received eight Nobel Peace Prizes for his efforts because he claimed to have ended eight ongoing conflicts. The president did not make mention of the war in Ukraine, which has raged on through his presidency as his administration has failed to bring the conflict to an end. And in the Middle East, the president earlier this year launched a war with Iran that is ongoing.

Trump said the committee's choice to award the prize to Pillay "is just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country."

Throughout his second term, the president has made clear his ambition to secure a Nobel Peace Prize, and his allies have said he deserves it for efforts to end the war in Gaza in addition to other conflicts. Earlier this year, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado, the 2025 winner, offered to share her prize with him as she sought his support for her efforts in Venezuela after the Trump administration removed former President Nicolás Maduro from power.

After learning of her award at a law gathering in Germany on Friday, Pillay joked to the crowd: "If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump."

The president was in Syracuse to boost the candidacy of GOP gubernatorial nominee Bruce Blakeman and state Republicans. He shouted out Saritha Komatireddy, the Republican nominee for state attorney general too, before attacking sitting state Attorney General Letitia James, a Democrat he has often clashed with.

"And on Election Day, New Yorkers should tell both [Gov. Kathy] Hochul and that disgusting Letitia dog — she's a dog — you're fired. Get the hell out of here."

The Trump administration has so far failed multiple times in its efforts to prosecute James, who spearheaded an investigation into his business dealings that led to a state judge ruling he had conspired to manipulate his net worth and ordering him to pay a fine of more than $350 million. The fine was later thrown out on appeal by a state court.

"Donald Trump is in Syracuse supporting the only attorney general candidate who clerked for Brett Kavanaugh, the man who ended Roe v. Wade," a James campaign spokesperson said in response to the president's comments. "The contrast is crystal clear and we welcome it."

articles.title: Liberal hot spot residents can’t agree on what socialism means as far-left movements gains steam
articles.summary: A Gallup poll shows 43% of Americans view socialism positively, but festivalgoers in Takoma Park hesitated when asked about surrendering property.
articles.body: Americans can't seem to get on the same page when it comes to what defines socialism even though new polling shows the movement's favorability is at an all-time high. Whether far-left factions are able to rally around the label could come down to understand its principles. Fox News Digital took to the streets of a Maryland liberal hotspot, Takoma Park, for its annual street festival to talk with attendees about their definitions of socialism and how far they would be willing to go to embrace its ideals. "The fact is that there's no…one answer," Nina Gilden Seavey said when asked to define socialism. "Just the idea of like, you've been paying all these things to set up these programs and then you're actually giving them to the people," Jaw Blake said describing his view of the political movement. "It's not a special group that gets to have them, it's just available." LIBERAL HAVEN FESTIVAL-GOERS WEIGH GOVERNMENT SEIZURE OF THEIR HOMES: 'I'D BE SO GAME' Jenny Sniderman had a more direct answer, claiming that "public libraries, the police department, the fire department, all our public services, utilities," are all part of what makes up socialism. A September Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans have a positive image of socialism — the highest level since the polling organization began tracking the question in 2010. But the survey asks respondents their image of socialism without providing a definition of the ideology or asking whether they would actually support adopting it in the U.S. The same festival-goers were pressed on socialism as an economic system, questioning their favorability of collective ownership. They shared some skepticism when Fox News Digital asked whether they would personally surrender their private property to government or collective control. "Do I want to give up my private property? Of course I don't want to give up my private property," Sniderman said. "Are they going to reimburse me fairly? That would be helpful in making my choice." "I don't know that I would necessarily love it," Blake said. "But I mean, if it was something that was beneficial, I'd at least consider it." DSA CO-CHAIR PUSHES BACK ON SOVIET UNION COMPARISONS, WANTS PRISONS TO BE 'LESS NECESSARY' "Nobody wants what they have to be taken away from them," he continued. "But there is something to be said about…you can set up things so that they're available for everybody." "I think the government is not the greatest steward…of assets," Seavey said. "It's not to say that capitalism is somehow without flaw, but the fact is that there is an idealism that can come from thinking, 'Oh, if we had some more centrality, if…there was some kind of uber organization in charge of reallocation.'" Documentary filmmaker and self-described historian Seavey also questioned the idea of government control over private assets, but argued that the growing democratic socialist movement in the U.S. should not be confused with traditional socialism. "This is not socialism. This is democratic socialism. It's different. There's socialism, there's communism, there are all kinds of 'isms.' Democratic socialism is essentially what we have a growing movement in this country," Seavey said. "Socialism is where there is a massive redistribution of wealth. We are not having redistribution of wealth in this country." But the Democratic Socialists of America, the largest socialist organization in the U.S., advocates redistributing wealth from wealthy individuals and corporations to workers and lower-income Americans. The DSA also calls for public stake in major corporations and essential industries rather than private ownership. THE NUMBERS DON’T LIE. YOUNG AMERICANS ARE FALLING IN LOVE … WITH SOCIALISM The differing interpretations among festival-goers reflect a broader debate over what socialism means in America — one that has taken on new political significance as socialist candidates gain ground within the Democratic Party heading into midterm elections. In a 2018 survey asking Americans to define socialism in their own words, just 17% described it in terms of government ownership or control of businesses or the means of production. Another 23% associated it with equality, while 10% pointed to social benefits and services. Nearly a quarter could not provide an answer. Seavey argued that political labels themselves have distorted the conversation. "Let's think about it differently and let's take away these ridiculous stigmas that have to do with these crazy labels that we have allowed the right wing to foment onto the rest of America," Seavey said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP But as socialist-aligned candidates compete for office, the growing movement raises a question that favorable polling alone cannot answer: whether voters are embracing its promises on affordability and equality, or also support its broader proposals for economic ownership and control.

articles.title: Workers erupt over DC plan to bring robotaxis to city streets: ‘This is bulls---’
articles.summary: Protesters rallied outside D.C.'s John Wilson Building as council members weighed legislation to allow Waymo robotaxis on Washington streets.
articles.body: A new proposal that could bring driverless rideshare vehicles to the streets of the nation’s capital is causing an uproar among union workers, drivers and religious leaders who fear the technology could eliminate jobs. Protesters gathered outside the John Wilson Building as D.C. council members met to discuss legislation that would allow Waymo and other autonomous vehicle operators to offer commercial rides in Washington, D.C. The protesters urged the council to reject the legislation, arguing that an influx of robotaxis would displace rideshare drivers. "We came out here today strongly because we feel that these robotaxis will put people out of work," one protester told Fox News Digital. "And people need jobs." TERRIFIED PASSENGERS FILM WAYMO AUTONOMOUS VEHICLE DRIVING INTO LIVE FIREWORKS IN SAN FRANCISCO "I'm against robotaxis because it takes away from the community, it takes away from their jobs, it takes away food from their table," Frederick from Virginia said. He continued, "People need jobs to be able to support their family." "It's bulls - - -," Sabrina from Washington, D.C., said. "Let's not bring robots taking my neighbor's jobs. My folks that drive for a living, let's just not take their jobs." Another person at the protest acknowledged that autonomous vehicles could eliminate some driving jobs but argued the city should "take the offensive" by shortening the workweek without cutting pay and expanding employment elsewhere. "We should take the offensive on job issues," Michael from Washington, D.C., said. "We should shorten the workweek, without a loss in pay. So we'll create more jobs in public transportation, in hospitals, in service industries. So we actually maybe will lose some jobs to taxi drivers, but we'll create better paying jobs." The Autonomous Vehicle Deployment Authorization Amendment Act of 2026 — introduced by Councilmember Charles Allen in May — would create a program for commercial autonomous vehicles in D.C. that would be run by the District Department of Transportation. TESLA ROBOTAXI MIAMI LAUNCH COMES WITH LIMITS Waymo says its latest safety data, covering more than 270 million miles of autonomous driving, shows its vehicles were involved in 82% fewer injury-causing crashes and 95% fewer crashes involving serious injuries or worse compared with human-driver benchmarks in the same operating areas. Supporters of robotaxis have also pointed to the potential for lower fares without a human driver, although current comparisons have found Waymo's prices can vary widely and are not consistently cheaper than traditional rideshare services like Uber and Lyft. Protesters claimed that while prices may be lower as the driverless vehicles roll out, the rates will eventually spike. "That's just something just to…get our antennas up and have us saying, ‘Yeah, ooo, we're gonna get cheaper rides,’" Sabrina said. "It might be cheap for the trial periods, and then all of a sudden we'll be paying $50. So no, I don't believe that. That's just some crap just to get people engaged with the Waymo." "They seem the same price to me," Helen from Maryland said. "They're in other cities and it seems like not much of a difference in the pricing." ZOOX ROBOTAXI REDESIGN BRINGS BIG RIDER UPGRADES The proposed regulatory framework, which could bring robotaxis to the city by 2028, would initially limit operators to 200 vehicles. Companies seeking commercial permits would have to demonstrate at least 180 days and 250,000 miles of autonomous vehicle testing in the District and submit plans aimed at reducing disparities in service availability and wait times across the city's eight wards. There was a public hearing on the bill in July, but no vote has been scheduled. The bill would have to be approved by the entire council before self-driving cars start to hit the city’s streets. "A worker should be at the table," Metropolitan Washington Council, AFL-CIO President Samuel Epps told Fox News Digital at the protest. "We shouldn't rush this." articles.title: Plague mystery revives concerns over not-to-secret Russian bioweapons program
articles.summary: Marshall Billingslea reveals Soviet defector Ken Alibek exposed a massive biological weapons program involving antibiotic-resistant plague research.
articles.body: Marshall Billingslea was a Senate Foreign Relations Committee staffer in the 1990s when he sat down with one of the highest-ranking defectors from the Soviet biological weapons program and began learning the extent of what Moscow had secretly built. And what he found out from Ken Alibek, the former No. 2 official in the Soviet biological weapons apparatus, is raising red flags for Billingslea over the Oct. 2, 2026, death linked to an anti-plague institute in Russia. "I think one of the most important things that Ken shed light on was the sheer scale of the Soviet program, which then Russia inherited," Billingslea told Fox News Digital. "Just mammoth." Three decades later, the mysterious death of a researcher at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East has put new attention on what became of that program — and Billingslea argues the world should be demanding answers from Moscow. MYSTERY DEATH AT RUSSIAN PLAGUE LAB TRIGGERS SWEEPING PRECAUTIONS AS US WATCHES CLOSELY "It's not acceptable in this day and age for the Russians to have a biological warfare program," said Billingslea, who previously served as President Donald Trump's special presidential envoy for arms control. "They need to cut it out, and they need to tell us. They need to come clean about what they're doing at this lab and whether this lab is still involved in their warfare program." The U.S. government says Russia's offensive biological weapons program did not disappear with the Soviet Union. "Russia maintains an offensive biological weapons program and is in violation of its obligations under the BWC," a State Department official told Fox News Digital this week. BWC, or Biological Weapons Convention, is an international treaty that prohibits the development, production and stockpiling of biological weapons. State's 2025 arms control compliance report assessed that the Soviet-era program was "absorbed, not dismantled" by Russia after the collapse and has "continued and evolved" since then. There is no evidence linking the Irkutsk researcher's death to Russia's biological weapons program, and Billingslea told Fox News Digital he has seen no evidence that the the institute remains involved in the program today. But the unexplained death has revived scrutiny of the Soviet program's work and the network of ostensibly civilian laboratories that Billingslea said Alibek identified as also performing classified work. Alibek's disclosures included Soviet efforts to alter pathogens to make them more lethal, transmissible or difficult to treat, Billingslea said, adding that some of the most troubling revelations involved plague. BIOWEAPON THREAT EXPOSED AS ANTHROPIC SOUNDS ALARM ON FOREIGN ACTORS PLOTTING VIRUS EXPERIMENTS "The goal was to render the plague bacteria far more resistant to antibiotics," he said. Billingslea said Soviet researchers also experimented with combining plague with toxin-producing pathogens, with the aim of making infections even harder to treat. "They took the plague bacteria and they merged it with a non-dangerous bacteria," Billingslea said. "The goal was to render the plague bacteria far more resistant to antibiotics." According to Alibek's account, researchers also worked on combining plague with toxin-producing pathogens so that treating an infected person with antibiotics could trigger the release of toxins. Billingslea said that U.S. officials were not relying solely on Alibek for their understanding of the program and that there were "multiple other sources of information" that made him "very confident in the basics" regarding the disclosures regarding Soviet-era research. "So this doesn't all derive from Ken Alibek," he insisted when speaking with Fox News Digital. By the time Billingslea was interviewing Alibek in the mid-1990s, he said, Washington had already confronted Moscow over its biological weapons work. "We knew about the plague programs, we knew what they were up to, and we knew where the sites were," he said. Among the facilities Alibek identified were at least six Soviet Ministry of Health laboratories that had legitimate civilian public-health missions while also performing classified work connected to the biological weapons program, according to Billingslea. The Irkutsk institute was among the facilities Alibek identified, but Billingslea cautioned he does not recall the Soviet defector saying that antibiotic-resistant plague or plague chimeras were specifically developed there. That distinction has become particularly important following the unexplained death of a 28-year-old researcher at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute. Russian authorities have said they found no microorganism linked to the woman's professional activities, while the World Health Organization has sought additional information from Moscow about what caused her fatal pneumonia. Billingslea said the pressure for answers — and for Russia to end its offensive biological weapons program — should not come from Washington alone. "It's very, very important that this is not viewed as a U.S. versus Russia discussion," he said. "This is a topic of grave concern to the entire international community." He also said that Russia needs to release the genetic sequence of the pathogen that killed the researcher, along with information about contact testing, the timeline of her illness and the institute's biosafety procedures. The genetic sequence could allow outside experts to determine "what it was and whether it was modified," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Billingslea called on countries outside the traditional U.S. alliance system, including Brazil and Mexico, to press Moscow for greater transparency, and pointed to a December meeting of parties to the Biological Weapons Convention as an opportunity for countries to confront Russia over the program. "At the December meeting, Russia is going to get grilled," he said. "And they should."

articles.title: A clock change dilemma pits science vs. politics
articles.summary: Some politicians want permanent daylight saving time, but a chorus of scientists say that's the wrong way to fix the seasonal time change problem.
articles.body:
Daylight is already fading, and soon Americans will set back the clocks too. But this year political support is building for doing away with seasonal time changes by switching to permanent daylight saving time.

That would be a mistake, scientists say.

A new report echoes a chorus of scientific research saying that permanent standard time is the best solution for eliminating the dreaded twice-yearly clock change.

You might enjoy daylight saving time for its later sunsets throughout the year. But standard time's earlier sunrises are more in line with our body clocks, leading to better sleep and mood, authors of the report say.

For now, most of the nation is scheduled to set the clocks back Nov. 1, ending daylight saving time and returning to standard time. (All states except Arizona and Hawaii currently follow daylight saving time.)

The new analysis reviewed evidence on the public health implications of establishing permanent standard time and permanent daylight saving time. Though the analysis is Canadian, co-author Ralph Mistlberger said it can be applied to the United States and much of the research reviewed was conducted in the United States.

"Morning light is the primary environmental time cue that aligns our biological clocks to local time. If morning light is delayed, our clocks and all the rhythms they control are delayed," Mistlberger told USA TODAY in an email.

Both choices have trade-offs. According to the analysis, permanent daylight saving time keeps evenings lighter, which may support recreation, social activity, commuting and some economic activity. But it also pushes sunrise an hour later, leaving more people waking, traveling to school and commuting to work in darkness during the coldest winter days.

Permanent standard time, on the other hand, preserves more morning light and better aligns clock time with human circadian biology, although evenings become darker earlier.

Politicians rally behind permanent daylight saving time

For years, the beginning and end of daylight saving time has renewed calls to end time changes, leaving two choices: permanent daylight saving time or permanent standard time. Politicians, with the loud backing of President Donald Trump , have set their sights on making daylight saving time permanent.

The Sunshine Protection Act , which would make daylight saving time permanent and eliminate the spring and fall clock changes, passed the House earlier this summer by a bipartisan vote. But the legislation still must clear the Senate and be signed by Trump before it can take effect.

Even with support from Trump and lawmakers in both parties, Senate Majority Leader John Thune has questioned whether enough senators support the proposal to move it across the finish line.

Iterations of this legislation have failed to come to fruition in previous years. As it stands, no state can adopt permanent daylight saving time unless Congress passes a law to authorize it, but some states have adopted or considered legislation to make the switch if or when such a law passes. There are nineteen states waiting for such authorization, including some that would only make the switch if neighboring states also do, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures .

Sen. Tom Cotton, R-Arkansas, has been a vocal critic of the legislation. The last time the nation tried permanent daylight saving time in the '70s, it quickly changed course – children walked to school with flashlights and commuter trains were delayed, Cotton said in a speech opposing the Sunshine Protection Act in 2025.

Trump on Oct. 3, in a push for the Sunshine Protection Act, posted what he said was Cotton's personal cellphone number to pressure him to support the legislation.

"Arkansans don't want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I'll always put Arkansas first," Cotton said afterward.

Sen. Rick Scott, R-Florida, who sponsored the Sunshine Protection Act, has a different perspective: "For many Americans, an extra hour of daylight means more time to play outside with their kids, walk their dog, or spend time with neighbors," Sen. Scott said in a Sept. 7 post on X .

"Americans work hard, and they deserve more free time to enjoy all the outdoors has to offer," he said.

Why experts say standard time is better for your health

Twice-yearly time changes are associated with negative health impacts, and springing forward is generally worse on our bodies than falling back, Erik Herzog, a professor of biology and neuroscience at Washington University in St. Louis, previously told USA TODAY .

The shift in spring is associated with an increase in heart attacks, and car accident rates also go up for a few days after, he said. Ending time changes would be good for health, but it matters which year-round time is chosen.

According to the authors of the analysis published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal on Oct. 5, permanent daylight saving time would have a negative effect on the body's circadian clock. Especially vulnerable are children and teenagers, they said. As young people go through puberty, their sleep timing naturally shifts later but they still have to wake up early for school.

"Our biological clocks need morning light to stay synchronized with the 24-hour day," Mistlberger said. "Permanent daylight saving time moves that light an hour later just when winter mornings are already darkest."

Shifting light toward the evening, while favorable for later social activities or businesses attracting customers later, makes it easier on the body to stay up late and harder to wake up early, but morning commitments don't change. That creates what's known as "social jet lag," Mistlberger said. Social jet lag and sleep restrictions can result in a wide range of health impacts such as chronic illnesses, mood disorders and even cancer, he said.

Shifting morning light later means people get up and get ready for work in the dark. Children walk to school or wait for school buses with low visibility.

According to a September report by K12 , if permanent daylight saving time were adopted, 94 of the nation's 100 largest school districts would have students heading to school in the dark each winter morning. On average, there would be 117 mornings where students would commute in the dark, compared with 77 in the current time changes and just 35 if permanent standard time were adopted, K12 found.

"The attraction of permanent daylight saving time is easy to understand. People like more light after work and school," says Dr. Patrick Baylis, associate professor at the Vancouver School of Economics at the University of British Columbia. "But those evening benefits have to be weighed against evidence linking later solar time with less sleep, lower productivity, and worse educational outcomes."

We've tried this before, and it didn't go well

Past dabbles with permanent daylight saving time in the United States were not winners with the public.

We had "War Time" from February 1942 until 1945, when Congress made daylight saving time year-round during the war in an effort to conserve fuel. After that, states were able to set their own standard time until 1966 when Congress universalized national time.

Then in the 1970s, President Richard Nixon signed a bill to put the United States on daylight saving time amid an energy crisis. While the American public at first liked the idea, soon "the experiment ... ran afoul of public opinion," The New York Times reported in October 1974 .

Congress reversed course after less than a year.
authors: Doyle Rice and Jeanine Santucci, USA TODAY

articles.title: Former MN state trooper tears into Dems as Somali gang violence terrorizes Minnesota: ‘Where is Ilhan Omar?’
articles.summary: John Nagel, a former state trooper challenging Ilhan Omar, accuses Minnesota Democrats of being soft on crime as Somali gang violence escalates.
articles.body: Former state trooper John Nagel pointed the finger at his opponent, Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., and the Democratic Party for allowing Somali-American gang-linked violence to escalate in the Twin Cities. Residents of Eden Prairie and surrounding Twin Cities suburbs have been left fearing for their safety after a string of gang-related incidents this month, including the shooting of two teens shot outside an Eden Prairie high school football game and more than 100 shell casings recovered in a Bloomington neighborhood. "Where is Ilhan Omar in all of this?" Nagel, a Minnesota native who spent 30 years as a state trooper, asked in an interview with Fox News Digital. "I would think that as a congressman that represents this particular area that she'd be at these meetings or she'd have a statement or she’d be sitting down and saying, ‘Hey, how can we help this? How could we stop this?’ And I don't see her." OMAR'S GOP CHALLENGER COMES OUT FIRING WITH VOW TO CLEAN UP 'MESS' IN DEEP BLUE DISTRICT: 'PEOPLE ARE FED UP' Nagel accused other Minnesota Democrats, including Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty, of having their "heads in the sand" and preventing law enforcement from stopping the violence before it got out of control. "They're being restrained by politicians, people that are trying soft on crime, people that're trying to send somebody other than a police officer to take care of issues, and it's not working," Nagel said. Looking at the responses of statewide leaders, including Gov. Tim Walz and Attorney General Keith Ellison, Nagel said the majority of Democrats "don’t want enforcement." "The people do," he said. "They're tired of it." Democrats have been too lenient on crime for years, according to Nagel, which he said has "emboldened" gang members to break the law without serious consequences. "Because of how the Democrats have run Minnesota over the years, these gang members and then just crooks in general, they’re emboldened by this," he said. ILHAN OMAR ON TRACK FOR FIFTH TERM AS MINNESOTA VOTERS MAINTAIN FAR-LEFT STREAK Ramsey County Sheriff Bob Fletcher spoke at a press conference this week, highlighting that a "big chunk of the problem" is failing to hold gang members accountable, saying Moriarty's office needs to be more "aggressive" with prosecuting juveniles. In a statement to Fox News Digital, Daniel Borgertpoepping, a spokesperson for Moriarty’s office, said that no cases related to the Bloomington incident have been submitted for charging consideration, but "they’ll be thoroughly reviewed" if they are. Adam Abdihakeem Adam, 18, was charged on Friday in connection with the Eden Prairie homecoming football game shooting with two counts of second-degree assault with a deadly weapon and second-degree riot. "Mr. Adam will be held accountable," Moriarty said in a press release Friday. "Violence in our communities is completely unacceptable and it requires a professional, coordinated response, which happened here." Fletcher also pushed back on "East African" being used to generalize the gang members’ ethnicity, adding that "98% of these gang members are Somali" and that the broader label isn’t "fair." "I think we just have to say what it is and not run away from the term," he said. AMY KLOBUCHAR CALLS FOR MAJOR ANTI-TERRORISM INVESTMENTS AFTER ALLEGED MALL OF AMERICA PLOT Nagel said people are afraid of being called "racist" for referring to the gangs as Somali, arguing that law enforcement is simply going after those committing the crimes rather than blaming an entire community. "I mean, we have Latino gangs and Asian gangs and Black gangs, and we have Somali gangs. This is not being prejudicial." He said it’s a "Somali problem" because that’s "who's showing up." "It's ridiculous," he said. "I'm a police officer. I don't care who you are. I don't care what color you are." Nagel said a "gang task force" could be part of the solution and argued, "We don't need to pass any more laws. We don't need any more people asking for money to help their group. We need to take the laws that we have and prosecute people." As gang violence spills into Minnesota communities, Nagel said it can’t continue to go on like it has. "We need enforcement, we need arrests, and we need incarceration," he said. "Otherwise, this is going to continue to spiral." Nagel will face off against Omar and Independent candidate DeVelle Jackson in the upcoming midterm elections for the U.S. House seat representing Minnesota's 5th Congressional District. articles.title: Army caught off guard by Hegseth’s order to make firing squad execution public
articles.summary: Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s announcement that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood mass shooter would be shown in public caught people across the...
articles.body:
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth's announcement that the execution of the convicted Fort Hood mass shooter would be shown in public caught people across the Pentagon and the Army off guard, three sources familiar with the matter told CNN.

Hegseth made the announcement in an interview with far-right podcaster Jack Posobiec aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln on Wednesday, which he'd visited to give a speech to the crew welcoming them home from their deployment to the Middle East.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said during the interview.

That comment was the first time many in the Army and Pentagon heard about the idea of a firing squad's execution of Nidal Hasan in Texas being made public, and there were immediately questions about what "public" would mean. There are Army regulations about who can watch a military execution, including family of the prisoner and of the victims, media representatives and a chaplain.

But it was decided by Hegseth, acting Army Secretary Adam Telle, and Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell and his staff that "public" would mean it would be livestreamed, one source familiar said. The Pentagon then confirmed as much to the media, saying in a statement, "The Secretary is correct. It will be livestreamed. Details will follow."

The Army referred questions to the Pentagon, and a Pentagon spokesperson said they had nothing to add beyond Thursday's confirmation that it would be live-streamed.

The idea has shocked many service members and veterans and provoked a bipartisan backlash . Vice President JD Vance cast doubt on Friday that the livestream could ultimately go forward, saying he didn't know "if that's actually going to happen," but said if it was, "I'm not going to be watching it."

"It takes away everything America stands for when we do public executions," one Army officer with multiple deployments to the Middle East told CNN. "The generational harm caused by allowing troops in uniform to stand in front of a man in a wheelchair and watch him get shot to death is irreparable."

President Donald Trump welcomed the idea of a firing squad execution on Friday.

"We're giving a man the death penalty who killed 14 soldiers a couple of years ago. Death penalty through firing squad — and he deserves it," the president said to applause during a White House event honoring Christopher Columbus.

Trump told CNN-affiliate WSTM on Friday he was not involved in the decision to livestream the execution, adding, "but I understand the decision."

Asked about the livestream by reporters at the White House earlier Friday, the president said his administration would make a determination about it, while reiterating that Hasan will be killed and "through firing squad." He didn't answer when a reporter asked if he'd watch the livestream.

FCC chair Brendan Carr told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" it was his understanding that the execution would not be shown on broadcast TV – but that he would defer to Hegseth and "his decisions on how to move forward."

Many of the details around the livestream have yet to be finalized, and multiple sources told CNN that officials have been working to find answers since it was announced. A second source familiar told CNN that great care is being taken to determine which soldiers would fire on Hasan, taking into consideration the potential psychological impacts of doing so. A specific unit has been selected to carry out the execution, the source said.

Showing the execution on a livestream presents more challenges, the source said, including any effort to obscure from the public the identities of the soldiers involved. It's also unclear where and if the execution will be streamed beyond the Pentagon's own website. Broadcasters and social media platforms have strict restrictions on violent and disturbing content.

The first source familiar said there are still questions about whether soldiers can decline to participate, given that the military is moving forward with this as a legal order.

The second source familiar echoed the same, saying while many soldiers may have "taken a life in combat," this is a very different situation.

"This is a situation where the guy has done a very bad thing and hurt a lot of people, years removed," the second source said. "He's going to be immobile and put up like a target."

For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com

articles.title: Veteran shot 7 times in Fort Hood massacre has a warning for Americans planning to watch execution
articles.summary: A Fort Hood shooting survivor shot seven times by Nidal Hasan wants to witness the firing squad execution but warns against treating it as a spectacle.
articles.body: On Dec. 3, 2026, the U.S. government intends to take Nidal Hasan to a firing range at Fort Hood and publicly execute him. Few condemned men could make a more difficult case for mercy. Seventeen years ago, Hasan, an Army psychiatrist at the time, walked into a soldier readiness center at the Texas Army post and opened fire, killing 13 people and wounding 32 others. Now, after years of appeals, the Army is preparing to execute him by firing squad. And Americans will be able to watch on live stream. That last detail has transformed what might otherwise have been the long-delayed conclusion of one of the darkest chapters in the Army's history into a more uncomfortable question: How should a nation reckon with the gravity of taking a life, even when that life belongs to a mass murderer? For Alonzo Lunsford, a former Army staff sergeant who survived being shot seven times by Hasan, the answer is complicated. GOP GOV DEWINE URGES OHIO TO ABOLISH THE DEATH PENALTY, SAYS IT IS NO LONGER A DETERRENT Lunsford wants Hasan executed. He intends to witness it himself in December. He told Fox News Digital he would even prefer that one of Hasan's surviving victims or the relatives of those he killed be allowed to pull the trigger. Despite that, Lunsford says he has forgiven Hasan. "The weird thing about it, I've forgiven him because my faith does not allow me to heal and continue unless I forgive that man," Lunsford said. But forgiveness, for Lunsford, does not mean sparing Hasan from punishment. What troubles him is the prospect of turning that punishment into entertainment. "It's not a spectacle," he said. "There's nothing glorified in the smell of human flesh, blood and gunpowder. It's a smell you will never forget. It's a taste that you will never forget." "That's not something you sit around and say, hey, let's get some popcorn and look at this execution," he continued. "We as a people, we're better than that. This ain't no country where we do public beheadings and stonings and think it's fine." ARMY SERGEANT SENTENCED AFTER SHOOTING 5 SOLDIERS AND HIS MALE FIANCÉ AT FORT STEWART Lunsford was working at Fort Hood's Soldier Readiness Processing Center on Nov. 5, 2009, when Hasan, an Army psychiatrist, opened fire. He recalled watching Hasan kill a colleague before turning the weapon on him. Lunsford was shot above his left eye, fell to the floor and played dead before eventually escaping outside, where Hasan shot him again. "I've accepted the fact I'm gonna live with the pain for the rest of my life," Lunsford said. He has since found purpose in coaching basketball, mentoring young people and helping others struggling with their mental health. Lunsford said he doesn't want children watching the livestream, though he believes adults can decide for themselves whether to tune in. "This is not somewhere you all start throwing some meat on the grill, get outside and say, hey, we're gonna watch them unalive this guy by firing squad," he said. "Don't do that." "Don't do that because when you do that, you're dishonoring those that made the supreme sacrifice, those who are no longer here. Those are heroes." War Secretary Pete Hegseth has defended making the execution public, saying Americans should understand the consequences of Hasan's crimes. "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public," Hegseth said in an interview this week. "Because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things." Vice President JD Vance cast doubt Friday on whether the Pentagon would follow through with its plans to livestream Hasan's execution, saying he had no intention of watching it himself. "I see these announcements. I don't know that that's actually going to happen," he told reporters Friday. The decision for the first U.S. Army death by firing squad in 86 years to be live streamed has drawn opposition even from Republicans who support putting Hasan to death. "I absolutely support the sentence of death, but live-streaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," Rep. Austin Scott, R-Ga., wrote on X. Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., likewise said Hasan "should face the death penalty," but called publicly streaming it "beyond disgusting." "Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," Tillis wrote. "It should not be happening in America." The nation's Catholic bishops have gone further, opposing both Hasan's execution and the decision to make it public. "In no way can Hassan's actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, said Friday. "The public execution even of one who has done grave harm will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people." The decision has also raised a more immediate national security concern. Hasan, who was left paralyzed from the waist down after being shot during the 2009 attack, has previously spoken about becoming a martyr. Matthew Levitt, a former Treasury counterterrorism official and director of the Washington Institute's Reinhard Program on Counterterrorism and Intelligence, warned that making footage of his death widely available could give terrorist groups material to exploit. "It seems like a poor decision to provide terrorist groups with a video clip they can effectively splice into radicalization propaganda," Levitt told Fox News Digital. "There's no tangible benefit to live streaming an execution, and it may, in fact, exacerbate the terrorist threat." For Lunsford, however, the execution remains deeply personal. During Hasan's 2013 court-martial, the two locked eyes. Lunsford wants Hasan to see him again before he dies. "I want to look at him in his eyes. I want him to see me — man to man," Lunsford said. "My message to him: Dude, you failed." "I go where I wanna go, when I wanna go, how I wanna go. With no fear," he said. "I can go outside and just smell and listen to nature. You don't have that luxury." And despite everything Hasan took from him, Lunsford said he hopes the condemned man uses his final moments to repent. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "I want to give him the opportunity to, the last words out of his mouth is to apologize and repent," Lunsford said. "And be held accountable for his sins and for his crime. And I will be OK with that."

articles.title: America's truckers issue dire warning as soaring diesel costs threaten 'domino effect'
articles.summary: Truckers say diesel at $6.32 per gallon is slashing profits and cutting routes, warning of a domino effect that could ripple through the supply chain.
articles.body: American truckers are warning that sky-high diesel prices are eating into their profits and putting pressure on trucking companies to cut routes, raising concerns that some drivers could be forced off the road and the pain could eventually reach Americans at the grocery store. "Fuel prices is going up, the rates are not going up," Miami-based trucker Suave Dorsett told Fox News Digital. "So it's hurting our pockets real bad." The warnings come as the Iran war sends diesel prices soaring, squeezing American truckers even as President Donald Trump predicts oil prices will fall "like a stone" amid expectations that the conflict could soon end. Drivers told Fox News Digital the damage is already mounting, with routes being cut and smaller operators facing mounting financial pressure. Dorsett is among several truckers who told Fox News Digital that soaring fuel costs are cutting into their earnings and putting pressure on an industry responsible for moving goods across the country, with one driver reporting fewer routes and others warning that smaller operators could eventually be forced to park their rigs. THE OVERLOOKED WAY THE IRAN WAR IS MAKING GROCERIES, AMAZON PACKAGES AND NEW HOMES MORE EXPENSIVE The national average for diesel stood at roughly $6.32 per gallon Monday, according to AAA — up from about $3.69 at the same time last year, a jump of more than 70%. The surge has also eclipsed the previous record of $5.816 per gallon, set in June 2022 under former President Joe Biden as Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent global energy prices soaring. For Dorsett, who has been driving for nine years, the price at the pump was even steeper. He told Fox News Digital he was seeing diesel at $7.40 per gallon while traveling through Ohio. Dorsett said the fuel spike comes as truckers are already shouldering a long list of expenses, including diesel exhaust fluid (DEF), which helps reduce harmful emissions, parking, showers, weighing and reweighing loads, repairs and towing. And if diesel prices remain elevated, Dorsett predicted smaller operators will be the first to buckle. BIDEN-ERA ENVIRO RULE ACCUSED OF STRANGLING TRUCKERS, SQUEEZING AMERICANS LANDS ON TRUMP CHOPPING BLOCK "Some of the smaller companies, like the smaller owner ops, would slowly fall off and it's going to create a chain effect," Dorsett said, predicting a "domino effect" that could eventually put pressure on larger carriers. Tyler Rinaldi, a Louisiana trucker with about a decade of experience who transports hazardous materials and other freight for an LTL company, said he has already seen weekend routes scaled back at his company. "I've seen a lot of routes get cut," Rinaldi told Fox News Digital. "They're not really running like they want to on the weekends right now." "I definitely see a lot change because of it at my company, slowly, but it's starting to be more noticeable," he added. TRUMP TAPS VETERANS TO FIX ILLEGAL ALIEN TRUCKING PROBLEM PLAGUING US ROADWAYS Rinaldi, who is married with two children, said fewer routes could eventually mean less money coming home. "When they start cutting routes and trying to limit the expenses on what routes they send out," Rinaldi said, "that takes away from the people that work in the company's pockets." Avante Jackson, an 11-year trucking veteran from Charlotte, North Carolina, who transports steel and other construction materials, said rising diesel prices are forcing truckers to take a harder look at whether the money they bring in is enough to keep their businesses running. "If I'm putting all of my profit in the tank," Jackson said, "at the end of the day, what do I have left to keep the doors open?" CUT THE BULL: THE REAL REASON BEEF COSTS SO MUCH — AND WHAT TRUMP IS TRYING TO DO Jackson cautioned against "fear-mongering" about potential shortages, but said a widespread loss of drivers could ultimately reach consumers. "It really could hit the community," he said. The latest diesel spike echoes a similar crunch in 2022 under former President Joe Biden, when the economic fallout from the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent fuel prices flying. Diesel reached a then-record national average of $5.82 per gallon that June, squeezing truckers as operating expenses climbed. According to the American Transportation Research Institute, trucking fuel costs surged 53.7% in 2022, helping drive a 21.3% jump in overall operating costs to a then-record $2.25 per mile. The latest spike threatens to revive those pressures, particularly for smaller operators with less room to absorb rising fuel bills. As the Trump administration pushes international partners to release emergency fuel reserves in an effort to bring prices down, the truckers had their own message for the president: don't forget about the drivers absorbing the costs on the road. "My message to President Trump would just be to think about who's keeping America moving," Jackson told Fox News Digital. "Think about the little guys out here each and every day." TRUMP JUST BROKERED A DEAL WITH THE COUNTRY SITTING ATOP THE WORLD’S LARGEST OIL RESERVES "We truly are the backbone of America, we keep America moving," he added. "We just want you just to think about us and put yourself in our shoes...Let's try to get the fuel prices down and let's try to just make more of a change," he said. "We know we can do better." Trump defended higher fuel prices Thursday as a temporary sacrifice in the fight to prevent Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons, saying on Truth Social that rising gasoline costs were "a small price to pay for Iran not having a Nuclear Weapon." Trump said last week that European countries had agreed to release diesel from their stockpiles after he pressed them to put more supply on the market. The G7 subsequently agreed to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products from previously pledged emergency reserves over four months, including a substantial diesel release during the first 20 days, in an effort to ease pressure on global fuel markets. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Trump also said his administration would not pursue a diesel export ban and expressed confidence that oil prices would eventually return to levels seen before the latest spike, though energy markets remain under pressure from global supply disruptions. Trump predicted during a Wednesday night rally in San Antonio, Texas, that oil prices would "come down like a rock" once the war with Iran ends, insisting the conflict would be over "very soon." "This week, President Trump signed an executive order that will quickly cut diesel costs and put money directly back into the pockets of American truckers, saving them over $100 every time they refill at the gas pump. Last week, he negotiated a deal with our European counterparts to release 100 million barrels—mainly diesel—from their stockpiles to add supply to the market and lower costs," White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers told Fox News Digital. "The President wants to see prices at the pump fall and continues to take historic action to ease temporary disruptions as oil flowing through the Strait of Hormuz approaches pre-conflict levels," Rogers added.

articles.title: Rahm Emanuel challenges DSA’s influence on Democrats, warns GOP ‘wing’ is disappearing
articles.summary: Rahm Emanuel warns the Republican Party faces a Mitt Romney and John McCain-style moderate exodus as the Democratic Party debates its left flank.
articles.body: As Democratic socialists, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, gain ground within the Democratic Party, former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel argued that socialists have less influence over his party than Republicans contend. Emanuel, the former mayor of Chicago and, at one point, President Barack Obama’s right-hand man, distanced himself from the more radical positions of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) while suggesting that the group could have a place within the party if it adopted more moderate positions. "I don't believe the socialists are a wing," he told the "Hang Out with Sean Hannity" podcast. "I think they are a separate party. They believe in defunding the police, which is not the party position. They believe open borders and open prisons. That's not the party’s position." RAHM EMANUEL WARNS ‘BERNIE BROS’ COULD SINK DEMOCRATS BY SADDLING MODERATES WITH SOCIALIST AGENDA "When you switch that, we can talk," Emanuel added. Conservatives have expressed concern over the rise of far-left, progressive candidates within the Democratic Party, warning that socialist-leaning politicians like Mamdani and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., could overtake party moderates. MAMDANI, TOUTING RI SOCIALIST’S VICTORY, ANSWERS QUESTION OF ‘WHAT IS THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY?’ Emanuel pushed back on the Republican Party’s characterization of the Democratic Party’s trajectory, pointing to New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger as examples of Democratic pragmatism. "I don't think that's where the party is," Emanuel said. "I think the party is in the pragmatic wing; you can see that in the governor of Virginia, you can see that in the governor of New Jersey, how they both won their primaries." FORMER DNC VICE CHAIR DAVID HOGG CLAIMS DEMOCRATIC MODERATES 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT VALUES' The longtime Clinton adviser argued that it is healthy for the Democratic Party to have debate between its progressive and moderate factions. He also warned that the Republican Party faces an exodus of its moderate wing once spearheaded by Mitt Romney and John McCain. "I happen to think we're going to have a healthy debate in our party," Emanuel told host Sean Hannity. "We haven't had it for 20 years." JAMES CARVILLE PREDICTS A 2028 'RECKONING' AS SOCIALIST CANDIDATES EYE THE DEMOCRATIC TICKET "There is a progressive and a pragmatic wing of the party. We'll have a healthy debate. That's what we should have," he continued. "In the same way that the Romney and McCain wing of your party is leaving. They have walked away, and that's what's going to tell the story of 2026." Emanuel’s comments come as he joins a broader group of establishment Democrats navigating an evolving Democratic Party, where Democratic socialist figures have gained prominence alongside the party’s more moderate tradition.
