Gavin Newsom is turning to former President Bill Clinton as his political model as speculation builds around his potential 2028 presidential bid, telling Vanity Fair Clinton is a "master of his craft." "I watch videos of Clinton. I seek his counsel, his advice, and even in his absence, do that. I’ve been a student of his from day one," he told the outlet.

articles.title: Sally Yates' Cornell alleged gang rape review could scrutinize crucial police interview, attorney says
articles.summary: Cornell University's Chi Phi fraternity case faces fresh scrutiny as Sally Yates examines a key police interview prosecutors never fully received.
articles.body: A key campus police interview that local prosecutors say they never received in full before initially declining to bring charges in the Cornell University alleged rape case could face fresh scrutiny as former Deputy Attorney General Sally Yates reviews the Ivy League school's handling of the allegations. Yates, who served as deputy attorney general in the Obama administration, has been tapped by Cornell's trustees to conduct a sweeping independent review of the October 2024 allegations involving members of its Chi Phi fraternity, after the university's own investigation resulted in expulsions and suspensions. The woman, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, told Cornell University Police during a November 2024 interview, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped," according to a transcript obtained by CBS News. She also described later sexual activity as coercive and said she had been "completely and totally incapacitated." Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten, however, said his office reviewed a six-page sworn statement that described Doe's participation in the sexual activity and drug use as voluntary and consensual. Van Houten said his office did not initially receive the complete interview and told CBS News last week that the information in the fuller interview "changes the landscape for me." INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM Scott Iseman, a New York attorney who has represented students accused of campus sexual misconduct, said Yates could review Doe's full police interview and compare it with her sworn statement, later testimony and other evidence gathered during Cornell's investigation. "Those full recorded interviews, I can tell you from experience, have a treasure trove of information that are really, really important to exactly what happened," Iseman said. "It wouldn't surprise me if there was additional information in there that would have changed the trajectory of this case because that happens all the time," he added. The apparent differences between Doe's full interview and her shorter sworn statement could be particularly significant, Iseman said. "Law enforcement is supposed to make sure that all salient facts are included in that sworn statement," he said. Cornell said its police department provided prosecutors with Doe's sworn statement and a Snapchat screenshot in 2024, describing the evidence-sharing process as standard protocol when a possible crime has occurred. Iseman cautioned that he had not reviewed the complete interview, which has not been made publicly available, and could not determine whether any omitted information was material. It remains unclear why the full interview was not initially provided to Van Houten's office. Fox News Digital reached out to Cornell University Police and the Tompkins County District Attorney's Office for clarification. Cornell said Yates and her team will have access to relevant records, case files, university personnel and leadership as they review the school's response, under its original Title IX investigation, which determines whether students violated university sexual misconduct policies rather than criminal law. Beyond the police interview, Iseman said Yates could identify witnesses who were never questioned, overlooked text messages or social media evidence, and other information that did not emerge during Cornell's original investigation. "There's a lot that potentially she could uncover," Iseman said. But he cautioned against assuming Cornell mishandled the allegations. "It may have all been done very appropriately by Cornell. We don't know yet." CORNELL PICKS FORMER DEPUTY US ATTORNEY GENERAL TO REVIEW SEX ASSAULT RESPONSE What Cornell's investigation found Cornell has defended its handling of the allegations, pointing to an extensive investigation that included more than 50 interviews and 12 days of disciplinary hearings. University President Michael Kotlikoff said two of the seven accused students were expelled, two were suspended for at least two semesters, one had graduated before discipline could be imposed and two were found not responsible for sexual misconduct. Cornell said both the accuser and accused students had opportunities to review evidence, testify and challenge the findings through an appeals process. What Yates' review could lead to Yates was brought in after the case erupted into a national firestorm following Doe's Sept. 16 lawsuit, which laid out graphic allegations that seven Chi Phi fraternity members drugged and sexually assaulted her during a night involving alcohol, drugs and group sex at their fraternity house in October 2024. The allegations have since sparked protests on campus while New York Attorney General Letitia James' office is conducting a separate criminal investigation. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men. Yates' investigation extends beyond the Chi Phi case to examine how Cornell handles sexual misconduct allegations across campus, including its oversight of fraternities, sororities and other student organizations. Her team at law firm King & Spalding will also assess Cornell's practices against federal and state laws and examine whether the university followed its own procedures in responding to the Chi Phi allegations. Any new or previously overlooked evidence identified during the review could potentially be shared with James' office, Iseman said, though Yates herself has no authority to bring charges. BAR NAMED IN CORNELL RAPE LAWSUIT DISPUTES ACCUSER'S ACCOUNT, SAYS SHE WAS NEVER SERVED ALCOHOL WHILE UNDERAGE Her findings could also lead to recommendations for improving Cornell's procedures, even if the university is found to have followed its existing rules. Cornell said Yates will report her findings and recommendations to a special committee of its Board of Trustees, which intends to share the results with the university community. Yates has tackled explosive misconduct allegations before. Her 2022 investigation into women's professional soccer exposed widespread sexual harassment, coercion and abuse by coaches, along with failures by league officials to act on complaints. What began as an investigation into individual coaches exposed much wider problems across women's soccer, prompting a series of recommendations for sweeping reforms that U.S. Soccer subsequently pledged to implement. Broader concerns The Cornell case also highlights a wider debate over the legal protections available to students accused of serious sexual misconduct, even as universities have the power to expel them. John R. Grasso, a Rhode Island criminal defense attorney and former police officer who has represented accused students for two decades, argued that campus disciplinary proceedings can carry life-altering consequences without offering the same legal protections available in criminal court. "When I defend a student on campus, we don't have any right to discovery. We can't compel the production of anything," Grasso said. He said those limitations can make it difficult for attorneys to obtain potentially important text messages, photographs and other evidence that might support an accused student's defense. Grasso also described the difficult choice students can face when university disciplinary proceedings and criminal investigations overlap: participating in campus proceedings and potentially making statements that could affect a criminal case, or remaining silent and risking disciplinary consequences. "I have a right to remain silent, but if I don't participate, I'm getting found responsible," he said, describing the dilemma he has encountered representing students. The human toll Grasso said the consequences of campus sexual misconduct allegations can extend far beyond disciplinary hearings, describing students whose education, reputations and emotional well-being have suffered even when they were ultimately cleared. "Bad things happen to the accused the minute a complaint is filed against them on campus. Really bad things," he said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP With the allegations now under renewed scrutiny, Iseman stressed the importance of keeping an open mind about what actually happened. "Just because the allegations are salacious or dramatic does not mean that's what happened," Iseman said. "So people need to keep an open mind."

articles.title: Trump: I ‘should have won’ Nobel Peace Prize, award is ‘forever discredited’
articles.summary: President Trump argued Friday that he should have been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize over this year’s Nobel laureate, former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge Navi Pillay. The president, who has long coveted the honor, was gifted the award by last year’s recipient, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado. In a late evening Truth Social…
articles.body:
President Trump argued Friday that he should have been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize over this year’s Nobel laureate, former International Criminal Court (ICC) judge Navi Pillay.

The president, who has long coveted the honor, was gifted the award by last year’s recipient, Venezuelan opposition leader María Corina Machado .

In a late evening Truth Social post after his rally in Syracuse, N.Y., Trump repeated his exaggerated claim that he has “settled eight Wars,” and said he was “about to settle, or win, two more” in Iran and the war between Russia and Ukraine.

“The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t,” he wrote.

“This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten,” Trump continued. “The Nobel “Peace” Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!”

In addition to her time on the ICC, Pillay served as a United Nations high commissioner for human rights and was the first non-white woman in South Africa to establish her own law practice.

She recently chaired a UN commission that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza, eliciting strong pushback from the Israeli government.

Trump claimed Pillay “very obviously, hates Israel” in his Friday post, and questioned her qualifications for this award.

“The Nobel Prize was given today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” he wrote. “In all of the Wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations—they were of no help.”

In a video shared online of the moment Pillay learned she was the recipient of this year’s Nobel Peace Prize, the international jurist joked that she “may share this prize with Trump.”

After Machado presented Trump with her award last year, the Norwegian Nobel Committee, which selects each year’s peace prize recipient, stressed that the prize was not officially transferred to the president.

“The medal and the diploma are the physical symbols confirming that an individual or organisation has been awarded the Nobel Peace Prize,” the committee said in a statement at the time. “The prize itself — the honour and recognition — remains inseparably linked to the person or organisation designated as the laureate by the Norwegian Nobel Committee.”

articles.title: These households could spend more to heat their homes this winter, federal outlook says
articles.summary: The fuel you use and where you live could have a huge impact on your heating bill this year.
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – While some households may spend slightly less on heating their homes this winter compared to last year, others may see price hikes of 20% or more, a new federal report outlines.

The U.S. Energy Information Administration this week released its Winter Fuels Outlook, offering projections of how much households will spend on heating costs and energy consumption. It takes into account the four most common heating fuels used and anticipated average temperatures across the U.S., as well as the potentially historic El Niño weather pattern (but more on that in a moment).

Energy prices and the local forecast impact just how much you will spend on heating your home this winter, the EIA contends. However, the agency overall projects that those who rely on either natural gas or propane to heat their homes “will have lower energy expenditures this winter.” That’s driven by lower fuel costs, according to the report.

Households using electricity or heating oil won’t be as lucky.

The EIA’s outlook suggests that, between November and March, those who use natural gas to heat their homes could spend about 9% less than they did last year, the largest dip across any fuel type. Those using propane may see a roughly 3% decline in costs.

Among homes relying on electricity, the cost may rise by about 4% this winter. In homes that use heating oil — about 3% of U.S. households — the EIA projects prices will jump by about 21% over last year.

The outlook notes that regional temperatures could have an impact on those average changes.

While “similar or warmer temperatures” are anticipated across the South, Midwest and Northeast, the EIA says the West could be in for a colder winter this year, causing some categories to swing higher.

In the West alone, households using natural gas or electricity could see their bills rise by about 7% and 9%, respectively, over last year. The year-over-year change is not nearly as drastic among other regions, the EIA report shows:

The EIA said this year’s El Niño weather pattern, which is shaping up to be the strongest in recorded history , “could lead to large temperature variations from our forecast.”

El Niño and its counterpart La Niña typically reach peak strength in the winter months. This year, El Niño is expected to peak between October and December. Last month , forecasters said that during that timeframe, “there is a 75% chance of a historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950.”

Whenever El Niño reaches peak strength in the winter months, it has its largest impact on weather in North America.

El Niño usually brings warmer, dry weather up north and to the Ohio Valley. Meanwhile, the southern half of the country can expect a wetter winter, with more rain and snow. The exact dividing line moves year to year, depending on the position of the jet stream. High-tide flooding may be a bigger problem during El Niño years as well, according to the National Weather Service, and especially on the West Coast.

Looking at trade wind patterns, Columbia University climate scientist Azhar Ehsan said in a September media briefing that this year’s atmospheric evolution looks similar to that of 1997, when one of the strongest-ever El Niños formed.

The super-strong El Niño contributed to chaotic weather from coast to coast. While the Northeast was hit with ice storms, the Southeast and California were drenched with flooding rain. Deadly tornadoes also tore across Florida.

One upside of the weird weather in 1997 was that heating costs were 10% lower nationwide compared to a normal year. That sort of savings might be welcome in 2026, as energy costs have soared .

A recent report from the National Energy Assistance Directors Association said U.S. households are projected to spend, on average, more than $1,000 to heat their homes this winter.

articles.title: Fetterman plays political maverick, but his voting record tells another story
articles.summary: John Fetterman votes with Democrats a majority of the time, yet his Israel stance and Republican friendships fuel intense party-switch speculation.
articles.body: The Senate's most recognizable rogue Democrat has increasingly broken with his party since Republicans took control of the upper chamber, but he still votes with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., a majority of the time. Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., is the Senate’s biggest enigma during a time of hyper-partisanship — he bucks his party on key issues, like the war in Iran and immigration, but continues to vote with Democrats an overwhelming amount of the time. Since joining the Senate in 2023, Fetterman has voted with Senate Democrats nearly 90% of the time, a figure that stacks up closely to some of the most staunch party liners in the caucus. Still, speculation has swirled as to whether he'll jump the political shark and become a Republican. MAVERICK DEMOCRAT SURGES WITH REPUBLICANS AS HIS OWN PARTY TURNS ON HIM, STOKING TALK OF GOP SWITCH Despite that, Fetterman has set the terms clearly this year, arguing that if Democrats continued to turn their backs on Israel, he would leave the party. But some in the GOP believe that no matter the swirl percolating in Washington, D.C., Fetterman isn’t swapping jerseys. He’s also keeping the speculation heavy about whether he will run for another term. "John Fetterman is a staunch Democrat that votes with his party 96% of the time, anybody who seriously believes that he is going to switch to the Republican Party is thinking wishfully," a senior Republican aide told Fox News Digital. Fetterman’s national political career began as a politician armed with an endorsement for Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., running in a pivotal race in 2022 against Dr. Mehmet Oz. SEN JOHN FETTERMAN PLEDGES TO BE 'LAST MAN STANDING' IN THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY IN SUPPORT OF ISRAEL Sanders told the Associated Press at the time that "if there’s any candidate who was running more than anybody else, who identified with the working class, who made it clear that he was going to Washington to represent working people, it was John Fetterman." He flipped that seat, giving Democrats one of the slimmest majorities in history and cementing himself as a rock star in the party. Since then, he’s run away from Sanders’ ideals and often rejected Schumer and the caucus’ marching orders. But this year he’s leaned into that grey area, sometimes known as being a centrist, to support Republican ideals. During this session of Congress, Fetterman has broken from Democrats more than ever before, dropping to just under 81% along Democratic Party lines. And while that's happening, Fetterman is reportedly using Republican fundraising platforms to soak up precious donor dollars, is close friends with one of the GOP’s own rock stars, Sen. Katie Britt, R-Ala., made a video message introducing McCormick at the RNC and even accidentally called himself a lifelong Republican during an appearance at the Texas Tribune’s Tribfest last month. FETTERMAN TEASES WHERE HIS TRUE LOYALTY LIES AFTER SURPRISE APPEARANCE AT GOP CONVENTION But when asked about whether he’s considering leaving the party, even after drawing a line in the sand, he recoils — it’s become such a hot topic in the hallways of the Senate that Fetterman stopped taking questions. As to whether he would jump ship depending on the outcome of the upcoming election, Fetterman said during the event that "there are no Republicans with a 90% Democratic vote line. There are no pro-choice, there's no pro-gay community, that does not exist in the Republican Party." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "How many times do I have to say it? And that's the point. So wait until after the midterms and see what happens," Fetterman said. "And now, if we do win, and I'm 51, people can remember, 'hey, that's why it's mathematically possible to retain the majority,' because I was able to win a state like Pennsylvania." Fetterman’s office did not respond to a request for comment.

articles.title: America’s adversaries are attacking sideways
articles.summary: A global system of allies also presents Washington’s adversaries with more targets.
articles.body:
When the U.S. imposed tariffs on China in April 2025, Beijing restricted exports of rare earth elements and magnets, threatening allied supply chains around the world in a campaign that continues to this day.

When the U.S. and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, Tehran expanded the battlefield to the Gulf states.

Last month, European Union defense ministers gathered in Brussels to grapple with the rising threat of grey-zone attacks. Even the normally taciturn Swiss government is raising the alarm about Russian actions. The August discovery of an explosive-laden drone at Germany’s Leipzig Airport underscores the larger pattern: Beijing, Tehran and Moscow are increasingly using horizontal escalation to challenge U.S. influence.

Horizontal escalation — the expansion of a conflict to new geographic regions or domains of competition — presents a vexing challenge for American policymakers. Washington tends to organize its policies vertically, into separate domains: NATO, trade policy and Taiwan. America’s adversaries are going sideways, operating across these domains rather than solely within them.

China, Russia and Iran differ greatly in their capabilities and objectives, but each seeks to overturn the U.S.-built international order.

Xi Jinping often speaks of “major changes unseen in a century.” In 2023, Xi famously invoked this same idea while standing beside Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow, exhorting the Russian leader, “Let’s push it forward together.”

To pursue their aims, America’s opponents sometimes cooperate. Tehran supplied Moscow with key drone capabilities when Russia was at its weakest in Ukraine. Russia, in turn, has provided Iran with sophisticated military assistance. Moscow is reportedly helping Tehran develop supersonic cruise missiles. China has helped blunt U.S. pressure on both Russia and Iran by supplying Moscow with essential dual-use items for its defense industry and by remaining a major buyer of sanctioned Iranian oil.

But U.S. adversaries support each other even without coordinating formally. Russia’s war consumes Western air defense missiles. Iran ties down American aircraft, ships and interceptors in the Middle East. China’s military buildup forces Washington to preserve scarce capabilities for a possible contingency in the South China Sea. Each of these efforts absorbs American resources that cannot be deployed somewhere else.

This exposes a vulnerability of American power. U.S. alliances multiply American strength and expand its reach. But a global system of allies also presents Washington’s adversaries with more targets. An opponent that is unable or unwilling to confront the U.S. directly can threaten a weaker ally, sabotage its infrastructure or disrupt its supply chains.

To meet this challenge, the U.S. and its allies must first deny adversaries easy opportunities for horizontal escalation. Diversify what is vulnerable, harden what cannot be diversified, build deeper stocks of scarce military capabilities and require allies capable of carrying more of the burden to do so.

But resilience should not be the only strategy. The U.S. cannot defend every vulnerability at all times, and trying to do so would hand its adversaries a permanent advantage. Instead, Washington and its allies should develop horizontal escalation options of their own.

Russian acts of sabotage against European infrastructure should trigger costs in domains the Kremlin values — weapons transfers to Ukraine, restrictions on Russian finance, seizures of sanctions-busting assets. An adversary may choose where to apply pressure, but it should not be allowed to choose where the consequences fall.

As EU Defense Commissioner Andrius Kubilius explained , “if we are facing painful hybrid threats or actions, our answer should be painful in a similar way … Not similar means [necessarily], but pain should be at the same level.” In the wake of the Leipzig incident, for example, Germany announced that it had shipped additional IRIS-T air defense missiles and attack drones to Ukraine.

This same logic should shape competition with China and Iran. Economic coercion need not be answered only with economic measures, and gray-zone attacks need not be met only at the site of the attack. America’s responses should create uncertainty in adversaries’ minds about where and how the U.S. and its allies will respond.

Horizontal escalation can also strengthen the bonds that connect U.S. allies. By imposing costs on countries other than the U.S., America’s adversaries may inadvertently provide Washington’s disparate partners with a common cause.

When China retaliated against U.S. tariffs by cutting European supply chains, Washington responded by forging a new critical minerals partnership with Europe. China’s support for Iran and Russia’s assistance to North Korea can likewise push the Gulf states and America’s Asian allies to reassess their relationships with Beijing and Moscow. In trying to expand a conflict horizontally, America’s adversaries may also be expanding the coalition arrayed against them.

Combating horizontal escalation will require Washington’s allies to guard against sabotage and coercion, assume a greater share of the deterrence burden and coordinate more closely to protect critical technologies and supply chains. But it also requires American leadership and dependability to ensure that openness remains a source of power for the West rather than a vulnerability.

America’s adversaries have learned to go sideways. The U.S. and its allies must show a willingness to do the same.

Peter Rough is director of the Center on Europe and Eurasia at Hudson Institute.

articles.title: Live updates: Trump headlines rally in Tennessee; Debate continues over Hasan’s execution livestream
articles.summary: President Trump confirmed Friday that he would no longer be attending the University of Georgia vs. University of Alabama football game in Tuscaloosa due to Hurricane Isaias, but still plans on traveling to Tennessee for a midterm rally. “I will go to Tennessee, where we have quickly called a Big Rally in order to get…
articles.body:
President Trump confirmed Friday that he would no longer be attending the University of Georgia vs. University of Alabama football game in Tuscaloosa due to Hurricane Isaias, but still plans on traveling to Tennessee for a midterm rally.

“I will go to Tennessee, where we have quickly called a Big Rally in order to get our fantastic Congressional Candidates, our Great Senator, Bill Hagerty, and a woman who will go down as one of the most impactful Governors in the State’s History, Marsha Blackburn, elected!” Trump wrote Friday on Truth Social.

The rally is expected to take place Saturday at 3:30 p.m. in Clarksville, Tenn., coming just weeks after he attended the Texas-Tennessee college football game in Knoxville. Trump also has upcoming rallies in Ohio and Alaska.

Also on Friday, before traveling to a rally in Syracuse, N.Y., Trump gave reporters mixed signals on whether Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan’s December execution will actually be livestreamed.

“Well, they’re making a determination about that, but he will be killed, it will be through firing squad,” Trump said told reporters. “He killed 13, 14 people, badly wounded 20-some-odd people and he’s totally nuts.”

Vice President Vance and lawmakers on both sides of the aisle continue to knock the event and say they will not be participating if a livestream were to take place.

articles.title: Socialists set sights on the ground floor of government as GOP warns of bigger plan unfolding
articles.summary: At least 65 Democratic Socialists of America-backed candidates are contesting state legislature seats, pushing defund police and reparations agendas.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — Dozens of individuals backed by the Democratic Socialists of America are set to appear on ballots as candidates for state legislature seats on Election Day, something Republicans say could set in motion a trend that transforms the Democratic Party. At least 65 DSA-aligned candidates have advanced to contest state legislative seats in November’s general election. The Republican State Leadership Committee — the official GOP body responsible for ensuring state-level conservative victories — claimed that these races could very well determine the future of the Democratic Party, according to a memo obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital. "The statehouse trend is also relevant because several prominent DSA-aligned Congressional candidates in 2026 have emerged from state and local political organizing," the memo reads. "These victories demonstrate one potential progression: movement organizations can help develop candidates locally and at the state level, provide them with political experience and organizational networks, and eventually support campaigns for Congress." SOCIALISTS CHEER ‘SHOCKWAVE’ PRIMARY NIGHT AS DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES WIN, ADVANCE ACROSS THE MAP "The scale of that presence matters not only because DSA-aligned candidates could influence the direction of their state legislatures if elected, but because state legislative offices can provide a platform, governing experience, donor networks and organizational infrastructure for future campaigns for higher office," it continues. The RSLC's methodology included candidates who are DSA members, DSA endorsees or self-identified members of the organization. DSA-affiliated candidates identified by the RSLC take positions on a number of issues that crucial swing voters and independents may find extreme, including defunding or abolishing police departments, left-wing economic policies and demanding race-based reparations. Opposition to traditional policing has emerged as a prominent issue among some of the DSA-aligned state legislative candidates identified by Republicans. "As a State Senator I will continue to do everything I can to end policing and incarceration in New York State," Democratic State Sen. Jabari Brisport’s campaign website reads. Brisport also supports decriminalizing prostitution, arguing that removing criminal penalties for sex workers while maintaining protections against trafficking and exploitation would help keep communities safe. TALARICO PUT ON DEFENSE AFTER 2020 COMMENTS ABOUT DEFUNDING POLICE RESURFACE: 'WE MUST REPLACE' Over in Wisconsin, Democratic State Rep. Ryan Clancy has stood by his statement that police work has "no dignity or value." "It means that American policing has always been bad and it always will be," Clancy told a local outlet in 2023, alleging that American police forces have their roots in slave patrols. "It’s not like we can get back to this to the early days… American policing… [is] epically racist and classist because that’s a dead end. That is the point of American policing." Clancy told Fox News Digital that his comments concerned officers who abused their authority over sex workers, although his original remarks and subsequent 2023 interview criticized policing more broadly as an institution he argued was inherently racist and could not be reformed. He concurred with the RSLC's assertion that DSA-aligned candidates are shaping the future of the Democratic Party. State Rep. Eleanor Chávez, running with the DSA’s backing in New Mexico, meanwhile has called Immigration and Customs Enforcement "fascist" and compared its agents to the KKK. Republicans in New Mexico have condemned such rhetoric, arguing that it could spur people to commit violence against law enforcement officers. Despite its propensity to draw attention to its stances on social issues, the DSA bills itself as an economically motivated organization. NEWSOM ADMITS DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST IDEAS ‘MAINSTREAM’ IN DEMOCRAT PARTY: ‘PRETTY ALIGNED’ To this end, some of its members running for state legislatures have called for reforms some have described as radical. New York Democratic Assemblywoman Sarahana Shrestha, who is running for re-election with the backing of the DSA, has pushed legislation that would allow the government to acquire the privately held Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp., potentially through eminent domain if a negotiated purchase cannot be reached.Dylan Wegela, a DSA-backed state house candidate in Michigan, has similarly pushed for state acquisitions of utility companies. Shrestha agrees with the RSLC's assessment that DSA-aligned state lawmakers could influence the Democratic Party’s trajectory. "The things DSA-aligned state lawmakers are fighting for are things that are extremely popular with voters, and have been for a long time," she told Fox News Digital. "A majority of our constituents believe the energy sector should not be for profit, healthcare should be single-payer and universal, the government should play a positive role in building necessary infrastructure such as permanently affordable housing and public transit, and so on." The DSA-affiliated lawmaker also defended her plan to take over the Central Hudson Gas & Electric Corp., citing a feasibility study commissioned by supporters of the bill that found it would lower costs for consumers. Sometimes, the stances of DSA clash with Democratic policy priorities. Gabriel Acevero, a DSA-backed lawmaker in Maryland, for instance, opposed a marijuana legalization measure he argued did not go far enough to address racial inequities, declaring that "cannabis legalization without reparations for communities harmed by the intentional drug war is not progressive policy." Scores of DSA-affiliated candidates running in states such as New York, Minnesota and Massachusetts have thrown their support behind reparations for racial minorities. SOCIALISTS ARE HELPING GOP CAMPAIGNS HEADING INTO NOVEMBER Republicans have a vested interest in tying the mainstream Democratic Party to the DSA. A Fox News poll from September found that 55% of registered voters had an unfavorable opinion of the DSA. While some in the Democratic Party argue that Republican attempts to tie the Democratic Party to socialism are bad-faith campaign tricks, party leadership has recently made significant concessions to its left-wing flank. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer backed Abdul El-Sayed's more moderate opponent in Michigan's Democratic Senate primary, but a super PAC aligned with Schumer has since committed millions of dollars to supporting El-Sayed's general-election campaign. El-Sayed is a progressive backed by prominent figures on the party's left, but who has said he is not a socialist. Due to the disorganized nature of the DSA and the varying degrees of affiliation held by candidates, estimates of the number of socialist candidates running for state legislature vary across sources. The Brookings Institution, for instance, found at least 76 had advanced to the general election, while the RSLC’s analysis identified a minimum of 65 running in a total of 24 states. Though the DSA's gains have received significant attention, a Brookings Institution analysis found that candidates backed by the organization represent only a tiny fraction of the nation's state legislative seats, raising questions about how far the socialist movement's growing influence extends. "The RSLC has consistently said that socialism starts in the states and that is where we need to stop it," the RSLC’s memo reads. "The DSA’s growing presence in statehouse races could have dangerous impacts for state policy in the short-term, and it reflects a clearly orchestrated long-term effort to build political power from the state-level up." articles.title: Democrats explode over Trump’s Russia diesel deal
articles.summary: Democratic lawmakers pushed back Friday on President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil amid global fuel shortages during U.S. military operations against Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war. The deal will permit Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government to supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace. “I have just concluded…
articles.body:
Democratic lawmakers pushed back Friday on President Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian oil amid global fuel shortages during U.S. military operations against Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war.

The deal will permit Russian President Vladimir Putin’s government to supply 300,000 tons of diesel to the U.S. and the global marketplace.

“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter,” he wrote in a Friday post on Truth Social .

It comes as the Republican Party faces growing discontent among the American public with rising costs of living under the Trump administration as it fights to retain control of Congress this November.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) accused Trump of making a “deal with the devil” in an attempt to save his “flailing political fortunes” in a Friday social media post .

“This filthy deal will only aid and abet the same Putin who is helping the Iranians to target and try to kill American troops in the Middle East and who illegally and viciously invaded our ally Ukraine,” Schumer wrote on the social platform X.

Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, described the move as “infuriating” in a short statement shared on social media.

“But this is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia,” the Virginia lawmaker wrote.

“Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake,” he continued. “Now he’s *lifting* sanctions on Russian fossil fuels.”

Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), a member of the Senate Judiciary and Armed Services committees, denounced Trump’s decision to lift the diesel sanctions, and urged the president to “rescind this agreement immediately” in a series of scathing posts .

“This poorly concealed attempt to mitigate the havoc caused by Trump’s illegal war in Iran will only benefit the Chinese & Russian economies & lead to the slaughter of more innocents in Ukraine,” he wrote on the social platform X.

Democratic Whip and Senate Judiciary Committee Ranking Member Dick Durbin (Ill.) accused the president of “considering bankrolling Russia’s slaughter of Ukrainian civilians.”

“Lifting sanctions on Russia will only fuel Putin’s war machine and prolong the conflict in Ukraine,” Durbin wrote on social media .

Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), a member of the Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, joined in on criticizing this deal, claiming Trump is “rewarding Putin with a windfall agreement that won’t even lower prices.”

Pennsylvania Rep. Madeleine Dean (D) cast the move as a “desperate” attempt from President Trump to “escape the consequences of his failed Iran war.”

“Trump is preparing to stab Ukraine in the back and buy diesel from Putin,” she continued. “He’s helping fund Russia’s war machine, while our allies pay the price.”

House Foreign Affairs Committee Vice Ranking Member Rep. Gabe Amo (D-R.I.) also slammed the deal in a social media post .

“After signing a law to ramp up sanctions on Russia, Trump is paying Putin for oil to deal with the high gas prices caused by his choice of war with Iran? That’s not punishing Putin, that’s profit,” he wrote, adding, “Make it make sense.”

articles.title: Key American industry seeing blue-collar jobs boom as Trump's re-shoring policies pay off
articles.summary: First on Fox: A CEA report says 72,000 manufacturing jobs were added in 2026 as reshoring and tariff policies reversed Biden-era offshoring.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: Critical blue collar manufacturing jobs in the U.S. are making inroads after years of Biden-era offshoring hollowed out the workforce, according to a new economic report. A Council of Economic Advisors (CEA) report says 72,000 manufacturing jobs have been added in 2026 alone, many of them due to a rise in the manufacturing of durable goods like metal and transportation equipment. The advisors say this is a reverse of a Biden-era trend that saw 200,000 manufacturing jobs disappear in the last two years of the former president's administration. Not only is the current administration's focus on re-shoring jobs contributing to the uptick, but so are his tariff policies, according to the CEA, a White House agency responsible for providing President Donald Trump with economic analysis. AMERICA’S NEW BLUE-COLLAR JOB BOOM IS ONE NOBODY SAW COMING — AND IT’S JUST GETTING STARTED In particular, Trump's landmark One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBB) has laid the groundwork for American companies to expand in the United States, instead of shipping jobs overseas, according to the report. The bill's provisions include allowing manufacturers an immediate 100% tax deduction on expenses related to new factory building, and purchasing machinery and equipment. The report highlights success stories from corporations that are reinvesting in Americans and expanding their businesses. LARGEST-EVER US STEEL PLANT IS COMING TO A KEY RED STATE AS TRUMP UNVEILS $15B INVESTMENT For example, the 100% expensing provision in the OBBB has helped Jergens, a manufacturing company based in Ohio, expand to Illinois. "Since the passage of the bill [OBBB], our employees are voluntarily working additional hours," the company's CEO, Jack Schron, said. "They are keeping more of what they earn, putting more money back into the American economy and Jergens has a ready workforce. It is a win-win-win: a win for the employee, for Jergens and for the United States economy." BESSENT CREDITS TRUMP IMMIGRATION POLICIES WITH HELPING RETURN JOBS TO AMERICANS AS WAGE GAINS RESUME Schron added that 83% of his workers are picking up overtime after the OBBB provision established no taxes for overtime work. In another example touted in the CEA report, a company in North Carolina, Ketchie Inc., has expanded its workforce by 25% after taking advantage of the 100% expensing provision to purchase new machinery. The report says the company waited to buy the equipment until the OBBB passed. As for wages, manufacturing workers are seeing benefits, too, with their pay increasing by 7.9% since January 2025. "Adjusted for inflation, this means that blue-collar manufacturing workers are earning nearly $2,500 more per year, on average, since President Trump took office," the report says. It also touts figures from the construction industry, including 100,000 construction jobs added since Trump took office. Semiconductor chip manufacturing, an industry in which the United States typically competes with China, is on the rise in the United States too. Micron is building memory chip plants in Idaho, Virginia and New York, which the report says is a $250 billion investment in the United States. Apple is investing $600 billion in American semiconductor production, too. The report also says that major pharmaceutical companies like GSK and Gilead are investing billions of dollars in the United States, along with automakers like Stellantis. PESSIMISTS SAY THE ECONOMY IS WEAK. THE GOOD NEWS IS, THEY ARE WRONG All told, the reshoring and tariff policies have resulted in $11 trillion in investments in the United States during Trump's second term in office, according to the report. Meanwhile, the economy is on everyone's mind with only a few weeks left until the midterm elections. Inflation, particularly high gas and grocery prices, continue to impact Americans before they head to the polls. Majorities also view housing costs (54%, down from 60%) and grocery prices (62%, down from 66%) as major problems. Nearly two-thirds of Americans say the economy is worse under the Trump administration than before.

articles.title: Special counsel gone wild: Jack Smith makes a splash at a ‘No Kings’ concert
articles.summary: It was vintage Smith — an almost mocking arrogance in the face of growing criticism over his methods and partisanship.
articles.body:
After his recent congressional testimony, former Special Counsel Jack Smith recently appeared at a “Power to the People Fest” sporting a “No Kings” tee shirt. Aside from a midlife crisis, the most likely explanation is that Smith wanted to send a message, reaffirming his bona fides as an anti-Trump warrior.

It was a Comey moment, but without the seashells .

The Power to the People Fest featured many whom Smith has long cultivated in the “Democracy-is-Ending” crowd. The organizers billed the event as “working to restore and strengthen democracy” and featured some of Trump’s loudest critics.

The top billing went to Bruce Springsteen, who has lately turned his concerts into anti-Trump rave sessions, including comparing Trump officials to “Gestapo” and calling the administration “treasonous.” He continued those attacks at the concert with Smith, denouncing Trump as “lawless” and this administration as murderers.

For his part, Tom Morello, the chief organizer of the rally, has called Trump and his administration “fascists” and leading crowds in chants of “F— Trump.”

And there was Smith in his own “No Kings” tee shirt.

It was a particularly inopportune time, as new evidence on Capitol Hill showed how Smith not only seized phone records of Republican members of Congress, but tracked communications with Trump’s attorney.

Smith has always been undone by his excessive appetite and his habitual failure to respect the limits on his authority. He has a history of losing major cases by advancing excessive and abusive legal claims. This included his stinging defeat in a unanimous Supreme Court decision dismantling his case against former Virginia Gov. Bob McDonnell (R).

During the Trump investigation, Smith showed that he had learned nothing from his losses. Indeed, former Attorney General Merrick Garland appointed Smith with full knowledge of his past disregard for constitutional limits.

Smith richly deserves to be criticized for his unrelenting attack on free speech protections as well as his decision to file a second case focusing on the 2020 election. And the unfolding details of how Smith seized the telephone records of Republican members of Congress, including those investigating his own conduct, only confirm suspicions that Smith wanted to bag Trump at any cost. That included seeking to curtail appeals and rush prosecutions before the 2024 election. Smith failed when Trump chose to run despite the lawfare, and he failed again when Trump handily won the election. But Smith’s obsession was so consuming that he was willing to try Trump right up to Inauguration Day.

The new details of Smith’s investigation should outrage members of both parties. The use of pen registers (to identify the destination of outbound calls and messages) and of trap and trace orders (for incoming) entirely disregarded longstanding rules protecting the legislative branch from such encroachments. And what is particularly alarming is that these searches were obvious fishing expeditions — these were not focused searches on specific wrongdoing, like the searches involving the corruption case against Rep. William Jefferson (D-La.) 20 years ago.

In addition to members of Congress, Smith and his team monitored the activities of Trump’s legal defense team, journalists and campaign advisers. That includes now-White House chief of staff Susie Wiles’ phone. At the same time, Smith secured a non-disclosure order from the court that prevented mobile carriers from notifying the affected lawmakers that they were being spied on. Thus, as members were looking into Smith’s excesses, they were not told that he was receiving and poring over their telephone records.

The White House Government Transparency Task Force released material this week showing that Smith’s team used an investigation codenamed “Plasmic Echo” to engage in an untethered fishing expedition. Notably, Attorney General Merrick Garland and Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco signed off on the sweeping seizure with no apparent effort to address obvious constitutional concerns over the right to counsel and Article I powers. Once again, Garland was entirely passive and simply endorsed the recommendations of those around him.

FBI Director Christopher Wray sent a March 2022 memo to Garland and Monaco seeking the attorney general’s approval to launch Plasmic Echo. Monaco added her endorsement before Garland signed off.

FBI investigators traced “Wiles’ phone calls and text messages with at least 21 lawyers affiliated with Trump, numerous campaign staff, political advisors, and at least five journalists from at least February to May 2023.”

This investigation also involved gathering intelligence on Trump’s political action committee, including its donors and campaign expenses.

Smith and the FBI continued the aggressive posture even as agents were balking at some of these means, including those who felt that the raid on Mar-a-Lago was unnecessary to resolve the concerns over the classified material.

Smith has continued to portray himself as unbiased and not motivated in any way by the election: “Anybody who has worked with me and knows me during the course of my career knows that I would not let politics play a role,” he has said.

But shortly afterward, he appeared in his No Kings tee shirt at the Power to the People fest. It was vintage Smith — an almost mocking arrogance in the face of growing criticism over his methods and partisanship.

The irony is that Smith was a better fit as a member of this profanity-spewing anti-Trump crowd than he ever was as special counsel. The pretense was gone, and he was finally in his element. In that sense, he might view this as his coming-out party, but Smith actually came out years ago.

Jonathan Turley is a law professor and the New York Times best-selling author of “ Rage and the Republic: The Unfinished Story of the American Revolution .”

articles.title: Talarico makes first appearance in 13-days at music festival after flu absence
articles.summary: Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) made his first appearance in nearly two weeks on Friday after his campaign said he was recovering from a bout of the flu. The Democratic nominee was seen strolling around Austin City Limits (ACL) — the annual music festival in Texas’s capital city. Videos shared on social media show…
articles.body:
Texas Senate candidate James Talarico (D) made his first appearance in nearly two weeks on Friday after his campaign said he was recovering from a bout of the flu.

The Democratic nominee was seen strolling around Austin City Limits (ACL) — the annual music festival in Texas’s capital city. Videos shared on social media show the candidate stopping to shake hands and take pictures with festival attendees in Zilker Park.

Talarico told a New York Times reporter at the Friday event he had been sick with a “nasty case of the flu” and had been “home in bed.” The candidate added he had more appearances planned for this weekend in Dallas.

His reemergence comes as both his GOP opponent, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, and President Trump have doubted Talarico’s flu diagnosis and called for the Democrat to return to the campaign trail less than a month out from November’s elections.

JT Ennis, a spokesperson for Talarico’s campaign, reposted a video of Talarico meeting with supporters at the festival on social media .

“Hate to disappoint the conspiracy theorists, but James is still alive and meeting with voters at ACL today,” Ennis wrote.

Talarico, a state lawmaker, holds a tight lead over Paxton in the Lone Star State’s closely watched Senate race this November.

Paxton responded on social media to a video of Talarico at ACL, saying his opponent “doesn’t get to reappear like nothing happened after ghosting the 31 million Texans he wants to represent for two weeks.”

“The ‘flu’ didn’t stop him from meeting with New York billionaires and Hollywood elites, or from partying with celebrities at a music festival most working Texans don’t have the luxury of attending, especially after taking two weeks off work,” he continued. “Must be nice after two weeks of PTO.”

Trump, who has endorsed Paxton and campaigned alongside him in Texas, criticized Talarico’s absence from the campaign trail in a Wednesday evening Truth Social post.

“Ladies and Gentlemen, upon information and belief, James TalaFREAKo, who is running for the United States Senate in Texas, is MISSING IN ACTION!” Trump wrote, using his nickname for the Democratic candidate. “He should immediately report to a Debate Stage against Ken Paxton, who is ready, willing, and able.”

Talarico has already agreed to several debates and called on his Republican opponent to do the same.

“President Trump just said Ken Paxton should debate. I agree,” he wrote on social media Thursday, adding, “Ball’s in your court @KenPaxtonTX .”

The Cook Political Report , a nonpartisan election handicapper, rates the open race to replace retiring Sen. John Cornyn (R) as a “toss up.” The Democrat has maintained a narrow lead over his Republican opponent, posting a 6-point lead within the margin of error in a recent poll from New York Times and Siena University.

I just get to continue doing what I've been doing, which is promote all of the things that President Trump is doing on behalf of the American people." articles.title: Forget the next big thing: How America’s old things keep us safe
articles.summary: Be it our military or our commercial sector, everyone seems to be pushing for the next new thing in America. That’s great, but what if the old things are ultimately more critical to our national and economic security? Take the Boeing B-52 Stratofortress, which has been in continuous service in the defense of our nation for…
articles.body:
Be it our military or our commercial sector, everyone seems to be pushing for the next new thing in America. That’s great, but what if the old things are ultimately more critical to our national and economic security?

Take the Boeing B-52 Stratofortress, which has been in continuous service in the defense of our nation for more than 70 years. Not only has it played a vital role in the war with Iran, but there are even plans to keep our fleet of B-52s active and combat ready into the 2050s .

Yes, innovation is always needed militarily and economically. But a cost analysis of keeping the old things up and running can not only produce taxpayer savings of millions to billions of dollars, but an optimum readiness factor needed to keep our nation secure as new things are dreamed up, built, tested and eventually brought online.

Another critical example of a desperately needed old thing is the U.S Navy’s fleet of Ohio Class nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines . Why is that class of submarine so critical? Many believe it served — and continues to serve — as the key in the U.S. nuclear-deterrent triad, which also includes the U.S. Air Force strategic bombers and intercontinental ballistic missiles. And yet, the most important piece of the military triad preventing a nuclear attack upon the United States is going on 45 years old and counting.

Innovation is not limited to bringing new technology and products online but also servicing existing and vital materiel. Unfortunately, many believe the People’s Republic of China is outpacing the United States .

Echoing this new reality was a piece in National Defense University Press, which highlighted evidence that “three U.S. military Services (Marines, Army, and Air Force) [are] probably logistically unsustainable.”

The piece then cuts to the chase with this observation: “This is even more disturbing because a survey of historical Great Power wars — and a specific study of China’s likely military options—strongly suggests that logistics is likely to be the primary determinant of military success or failure.”

In the greater world of logistics, it is often the little things that matter but don’t get the needed recognition or priority. I was reminded of this during a recent conversation with an Air Force general, who stressed repeatedly that acquisition costs pale in comparison to lifecycle costs.

He gave an example that had never crossed my mind, and I suspect I’m not alone: the vital need to replace old rivets (fasteners) in collectively thousands of military and commercial aircraft. It’s something the People’s Republic of China already excels at. Fortunately, the general stated that they have identified a state-of-the-art technology that can replace old fasteners 20 times more efficiently via robotics.

Faster, cheaper, better and safer is a critical advantage in the growing logistics war against China. Be it the replacement of millions of old rivets on aircraft or the continual updating of our submarine fleet, keeping the old things battle ready and up to date is mandatory when it comes to keeping pace with our nation’s number one adversary.

This point was hammered home in the conclusion of the National Defense University piece: “the U.S. military faces the greatest logistical challenge of its history, in a conflict where logistics is likely to be determinative. … To overcome these challenges, America must invigorate the culture, organization, and mindset of its logistics communities.”

Unfortunately, that message has not yet settled in among all the key decisionmakers. Maybe as they are traveling to their next meeting aboard a 30-year-old commercial or military aircraft, they might begin by focusing on the potential age of the rivets in the wings, then mentally work their way through the rest of the logistical replacement progression needed to keep the U.S. on top.

At that exact moment, the old thing might seem incredibly important.

Douglas MacKinnon is a former White House and Pentagon official.

articles.title: The Memo: Guilfoyle furor rises as Trump stops short of expressing support
articles.summary: The uproar isn’t dying down over U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and her reported request to have a MAGA donor pay down her personal credit card debt. President Trump, when asked about the matter as he prepared to leave for New York Friday, was conspicuously noncommittal. “I just heard about it: Too bad,” Trump…
articles.body:
The uproar isn’t dying down over U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle and her reported request to have a MAGA donor pay down her personal credit card debt.

President Trump, when asked about the matter as he prepared to leave for New York Friday, was conspicuously noncommittal.

“I just heard about it: Too bad,” Trump said , adding, “I don’t know too much. But she was always very nice.”

Earlier Friday, a similar question was posed to Vice President Vance. He said only “allegations” had emerged so far, and added, “We don’t try people in the court of public opinion. We try people in a court of law.”

Vance said he had known Guilfoyle — an erstwhile Fox News personality who was previously engaged to the president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr. — “for a long time.” But he acknowledged that “obviously if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it.”

Neither Trump’s nor Vance’s comments equated to a forceful vote of confidence in Guilfoyle, who is also the ex-wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D). Guilfoyle and Newsom divorced 20 years ago.

The bigger political question is whether the story will become part of a larger narrative of alleged unethical behavior on the part of the Trump administration as the midterms near.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor who is exploring a 2028 presidential bid, wrote on social media that the reports about Guilfoyle’s behavior were part of a larger picture that showed how “the cost of doing business with the Trump Admin 2.0 really adds up.”

Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), seeking reelection in a competitive state , told MS NOW’s “The Briefing With Jen Psaki” Thursday that Guilfoyle was “partying across Europe after begging donors to bail her out financially and conducting herself in a way that appears to be deeply unethical.”

Ossoff also raised the possibility of congressional investigations into Guilfoyle if Democrats take back control of the House.

On that score, Democrats on the House Oversight Committee sent Guilfoyle a letter Thursday requesting the ambassador preserve her records and provide any communications with key figures in the matter.

The ranking Democrat on the committee, Rep. Robert Garcia (Calif.), wrote that “the alleged misconduct raises serious public corruption and national security concerns.” The letter was first reported by PBS News.

The Guilfoyle controversy first erupted Wednesday with a remarkable Wall Street Journal story .

The Journal reviewed text messages between Guilfoyle and Eric Deters, a pro-Trump businessman and former lawyer who has in the past run unsuccessfully for a House seat and for the governorship of Kentucky.

One exchange showed Guilfoyle apparently seeking $100,000 from Deters to alleviate debt with American Express. “It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she wrote on Signal, the Journal reported. “Please.”

The messages also appeared to show an awareness on Guilfoyle’s part that the communications between her and Deters could prove damaging.

“Eric, I really wish you would stop papering all these things,” she wrote in one message, saying it would be better if he were to “simply just call me on signal.”

Deters says he was seeking Guilfoyle’s assistance on at least two matters: a probe into his tax deductions, about which he wanted to speak with then-incoming IRS Commissioner Billy Long , and his desire to have an Ohio doctor extradited back to the U.S. from Pakistan.

Deters did not ultimately pay the $100,000 credit card debt. But he did separately tell Guilfoyle he had “paid you $300,000 over the years,” had “not received one favor” and needed to see “results.”

The Journal also noted: “Jesse Binnall, a lawyer for Guilfoyle, said the ambassador disputed the authenticity of the messages but declined to provide specifics.” The lawyer also told the Journal Deters had legitimately owed money to Guilfoyle relating to speaking engagements.

This is the second time a major report from the Wall Street Journal has raised questions about Guilfoyle’s conduct. An extensive story late last month investigated her apparent closeness with a lobbyist for a Greek company.

The latest story created a major headache for Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who was in Greece when it broke. The centerpiece of Rubio’s trip was intended to be a speech about the importance of upholding Western values.

Instead, he found himself on one occasion declining to comment on the Guilfoyle furor while a Greek minister looked on and on another getting into a testy exchange with reporters in which he told them , “I know the game.”

It’s possible the Trump administration will simply hope the matter fades away, supplanted in the news agenda by other stories. But even some Republican voices aren’t sure that will happen.

“One thing that swing voters, in particular, are unwilling to do is vote for people who seem to be the more crooked of their options on any given ballot,” said Republican strategist Liz Mair.

“Do I think the midterms are going to turn on Kim Guilfoyle? No, I don’t,” Mair added. “But do I think this is an easier-to-understand scandal than some of the crypto scandals. Kim Guilfoyle asking a donor to pay off a hundred grand of credit card debt is a lot easier for your average voter to understand.”

Grant Reeher, a professor of political science at Syracuse University, suggested the impact might be limited because questions around Trump family’s conduct, and people in their orbit, may already be factored into voters’ considerations.

“We already know this family have made themselves spectacularly wealthy just from being in office. There is no argument about it and Trump in fact has been very open about it,” he said.

The Guilfoyle controversy may not on its own lose any GOP candidate an election, she said, “but I do think it’s a big problem.”

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage.

articles.title: Who is Sally Yates? Cornell rape-review pick was fired by Trump after refusing to defend travel ban
articles.summary: Sally Yates, fired by Trump as acting attorney general in 2017, will now lead Cornell University's independent review of sexual assault policies.
articles.body: Cornell University has tapped Sally Yates, a former Obama administration deputy attorney general fired by President Donald Trump during his first term, to lead an independent review of the Ivy League school's handling of sexual assault allegations. Yates' appointment comes as Cornell faces scrutiny over its response to an alleged gang rape at a fraternity house in October 2024. As part of the independent review, Yates and her employer, King & Spalding, will have access to Cornell's internal documents, including case files, oversight records for Greek organizations, communications with law enforcement and disciplinary hearing records. Yates brings decades of Justice Department experience to Cornell's review, along with a public profile shaped by her confrontation with Trump and subsequent involvement in the Russia investigation. Sally Yates' career and clashes with Trump President Barack Obama nominated Yates as deputy attorney general in January 2015, and the Senate confirmed her four months later in an 84-12 vote. She previously served as U.S. attorney for the Northern District of Georgia, a position Obama appointed her to in 2010. CORNELL PRESIDENT SAYS UNIVERSITY 'MUST DO BETTER' ON HANDLING OF SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS During the presidential transition, Trump's incoming administration asked Yates to remain as acting attorney general while his nominee, Jeff Sessions, awaited Senate confirmation. But her tenure lasted just 10 days. Trump fired Yates on Jan. 30, 2017, after she instructed Justice Department lawyers not to defend his executive order restricting travel and refugee admissions from seven predominantly Muslim countries. "The acting Attorney General, Sally Yates, has betrayed the Department of Justice by refusing to enforce a legal order designed to protect the citizens of the United States," the White House said in a statement announcing her firing. Yates maintained that she was not convinced the directive was lawful. "My responsibility is to ensure that the position of the Department of Justice is not only legally defensible, but is informed by our best view of what the law is after consideration of all the facts," Yates said in a letter. "In addition, I am responsible for ensuring that the positions we take in court remain consistent with this institution’s solemn obligation to always seek justice and stand for what is right." Yates returned to the national spotlight in May 2017, testifying before a Senate Judiciary subcommittee investigating Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. Her testimony detailed warnings she had given White House Counsel Don McGahn about Trump's then-national security adviser, Michael Flynn, shortly before her dismissal. CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS PROMPT NY ATTORNEY GENERAL LETITIA JAMES TO OPEN ‘ACTIVE CRIMINAL INVESTIGATION’ Flynn had discussed Obama administration sanctions against Russia with Russian Ambassador Sergey Kislyak in December 2016, despite then-Vice President-elect Mike Pence publicly denying that sanctions were discussed. After reviewing FBI intelligence, Yates warned McGahn that Flynn had misled administration officials and could be vulnerable to Russian blackmail because Moscow knew what had actually been discussed. Flynn resigned in February 2017, 18 days after Yates' initial warning. He later pleaded guilty to making false statements to the FBI about his conversations with Kislyak. Before her confrontation with Trump, Yates spent 27 years at the Justice Department, prosecuting white-collar fraud and public corruption cases. She also served as lead prosecutor in the case against Olympic Park bomber Eric Rudolph, a prosecution then-Attorney General Eric Holder highlighted when Obama selected her as deputy attorney general. Yates returned to King & Spalding as a partner in May 2018, later leading an independent investigation into sexual misconduct and abuse in the National Women's Soccer League. Commissioned by the U.S. Soccer Federation in October 2021, the investigation included more than 200 interviews and uncovered widespread verbal and emotional abuse, sexual misconduct and repeated failures by teams and league officials to address complaints. The findings, released in October 2022, documented how coaches accused of misconduct continued working despite previous complaints. Yates' report recommended stronger background checks, clearer reporting procedures and greater accountability for teams and league officials. Cornell University investigations Cornell said it selected Yates and her firm because of "their expertise in higher education and extensive experience conducting independent investigations for boards and institutions." INSIDE EXPLOSIVE CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS: 7 MEN ACCUSED, CONFLICTING ACCOUNTS AND A POLITICAL FIRESTORM Yates' involvement in the case brings another prominent Trump adversary into the controversy, days after New York Attorney General Letitia James, who previously brought a civil fraud case against Trump and has faced his calls for her prosecution, was appointed to oversee a separate state investigation. Cornell previously investigated the alleged assault and imposed suspensions and expulsions on several students accused of involvement. A lawsuit filed against the university by the alleged victim has since brought renewed national attention to the case and raised questions about the school's response. The two investigations have separate mandates. James' investigation will examine the case at the center of the controversy, while Yates' review will assess Cornell's broader policies and handling of sexual assault and dating violence allegations. "As part of that broader mandate, Yates and her team will conduct a detailed review of the university’s response to the allegations involving Jane Doe and members of the Chi Phi fraternity in October 2024, including whether Cornell followed its policies and procedures in responding to the matter," the school said in a statement. articles.title: 9 people dead in Erie, Pennsylvania mass shooting
articles.summary: ERIE, Pa. (WJET) — Nine people are dead after what Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro described as a mass shooting in the City of Erie Friday night. The City of Erie also confirmed Saturday morning that nine people lost their lives in what they’re describing as a tragedy. According to the city, officers arrived on the…
articles.body:
ERIE, Pa. ( WJET ) — Nine people are dead after what Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro described as a mass shooting in the City of Erie Friday night.

The City of Erie also confirmed Saturday morning that nine people lost their lives in what they’re describing as a tragedy.

According to the city, officers arrived on the scene within minutes of receiving a ShotSpotter alert, and they say investigators found that all deaths happened before officers arrived. They also clarified that sounds heard during the police response were not gunfire. The city says those sounds were flash bangs from law enforcement’s tactical response.

Erie Mayor Daria Devlin’s office urged residents to “exercise care in sharing information,” citing “unverified reports and speculation” that circulated since the incident.

Erie police were called to the scene just before 5 p.m. Friday evening. Witnesses told police the gunman then ran into a nearby home.

Law enforcement first confirmed that two women were fatally shot on a sidewalk outside a home. Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah later confirmed that the shooter is also dead from what appears to be a self-inflicted gunshot wound.

According to Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook, two children were also found deceased inside the home.

Governor Shapiro released a brief statement Saturday morning, saying:

“I’ve spoken with Mayor Devlin and offered my Administration’s full support following the tragic mass shooting in Erie last night — killing nine of our fellow Pennsylvanians.”

“My heart breaks for this family. Lori and I are praying for their loved ones and the entire Erie community.”

Erie Mayor Daria Devlin is expected to address the city and provide more information at a press conference at 4:00 p.m. on Saturday.

articles.title: The fight for EPA workers’ rights is a fight for the American public
articles.summary: Federal employees do not work for a president, a political party or an ideology — we work for America.
articles.body:
Last year, the Environmental Protection Agency did something that should trouble every American when it tore up a legally negotiated union contract covering approximately 8,000 civil servants. The contract took years to negotiate and was undone in a single day, with claims that its protections somehow threatened “ national security ”.

EPA workers lost union representation in disciplinary proceedings, the ability to challenge unfair treatment through independent grievance and arbitration proceedings and first-of-its-kind protections for employees who raise concerns about scientific misconduct or political interference.

In short, an entire workforce lost its rights.

Last month, we took action. The American Federation of Government Employees Council 238 sued the EPA and Administrator Lee Zeldin to restore our contract and defend the rights our members fought for and won.

This is much bigger than a labor dispute. It is a fight over public health, the rule of law and what public service is supposed to mean in this country. Federal employees do not work for a president, a political party or an ideology — we work for America.

The American Federation of Government Employees was born in 1932, a precarious time for the civil servants as politicians tried to dismantle the civil service system. Decades of organizing eventually led President Kennedy to recognize federal employees’ right to bargain collectively in 1962, and to the implementation of the Federal Service Labor-Management Relations Statute , which declared that collective bargaining in the civil service “ safeguards the public interest .”

There is a reason Congress connected workers’ rights to the public interest. Federal unions give career public servants the independence to do their jobs when political pressure comes from above. Those protections give workers the backbone to tell the truth, do the job right and put the American people first.

That independence matters more than ever at the EPA. Climate change, pollution and even science itself has become more partisan, with powerful industries lobbying for policies that only serve their interests.

But there is too much at stake for science to be twisted or gagged for a political agenda or a corporate bottom line.

Our members are scientists, engineers, environmental specialists, enforcement officers, field inspectors, biologists, chemists, lab technicians and other professionals whose work directly protects communities. When a pollutant threatens children with asthma, when a community cannot trust its drinking water or when a wildfire leaves behind hazardous chemicals and contaminated runoff, EPA workers have a responsibility to follow the science, take action and protect the public.

Our union contract was built for exactly those moments. It protected workers’ right to follow the evidence, raise concerns about scientific misconduct or political interference and speak up when public health is on the line without fearing that doing their jobs could cost them their careers. It served as a safeguard for every American who expects government scientists to tell The unilateral termination of our contract throws all of that out the window, and we have already seen what happens when those safeguards disappear.

Just before our contract was terminated, hundreds of EPA employees signed a declaration of dissent in June 2025, raising concerns about political interference in science-based decision-making and threats to public health. The agency did not immediately discipline the workers who signed it. Instead, it moved to terminate our contract. Only after workers had lost their union representation and their ability to challenge discipline did the EPA punish the signers.

Ultimately, 139 employees were disciplined . Twenty were fired and 119 were suspended without pay. Of those disciplined, 110 had been covered by our contract.

This went beyond stripping away workplace protections. It violated workers’ First Amendment rights by targeting employees who exercised protected speech and spoke out on matters of public concern. It also sent a message: Speak out against political interference, and you could pay for it with your career.

What the agency failed to consider is that EPA workers are not intimidated. We do this work because we believe in the mission to protect human health and the environment. Thousands of dedicated civil servants make up this agency, and we are not afraid to take on this administration in court and in the streets to defend our ability to do our jobs. The stakes are too high to remain silent and cowed.

We also know this fight also reaches far beyond the EPA. The administration has targeted collective bargaining across the federal government, including at the Department of Veterans Affairs, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the Food and Drug Administration, the Bureau of Prisons and the Department of Defense. What is happening at EPA is part of a broader attack on a federal workforce whose job is to serve the public, not bend to a political ideology.

Public servants need to be able to tell the truth without first asking whether the truth will cost them their jobs and livelihood. We are fighting for our contract, but we are also fighting for a government that works for the people it serves.

Administrations come and go. Our responsibility does not.

Justin Chen is president of the American Federation of Government Employees Council 238.
